title: Beyond the Leapfrog Trap: The Critical Role of Employee Dexterity in Vietnam's Digital Future

detail.title: Beyond the Leapfrog Trap: The Critical Role of Employee Dexterity in Vietnam's Digital Future
detail.abstract:
Executive Summary: Vietnam is currently experiencing a macroeconomic "leapfrog" phenomenon, rapidly bypassing legacy technologies to adopt Cloud, AI, and advanced ERP systems. However, analysis reveals a critical disconnect: while Vietnamese enterprises possess the tools of a modern enterprise, they often lack the operational DNA to leverage them, leading to "ROI Paralysis."

This policy brief argues that without a pivot toward a human-centric adoption strategy, Vietnam's digital boom risks becoming a "Digital Facade"—shiny on the outside, but strategically hollow on the inside.

Key Findings: * The "Dexterity Premium": Quantitative analysis reveals that 66.1% of the strategic value of digital tools is unlocked only through "Employee Digital Dexterity"—the workforce's adaptability and willingness to leverage new tools. * The Culture Gatekeeper: "Hierarchy Cultures" (rigid, top-down structures) were found to actively suppress digital dexterity, whereas "Adhocracy Cultures" (flexible, decentralized) act as the primary catalyst for digital success. * Strategic Recommendation: To escape the "Leapfrog Trap," firms must shift budget allocation from software licensing to workforce upskilling and aggressively flatten organizational structures.

integrates prediction-diagnosis-measurement-intervention into coherent architecture while
preserving human dignity through structural rather than psychological explanation.

title: Property Rights in Virtual Things: Digital Files, Revisited
affiliations: Queen Mary University of London, School of Law - Centre for Commercial Law Studies and Queen Mary University of London, School of Law - Centre for Commercial Law Studies

detail.title: Property Rights in Virtual Things: Digital Files, Revisited

declarations.funderStatement: This paper has been produced by members of the Cloud Legal Project, Centre for Commercial Law Studies, Queen Mary University of London. The authors are grateful to Microsoft for the generous financial support that has made this project possible. Responsibility for views expressed, however, remains with the authors.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we explore whether English law can develop an in rem property right in digital files by analogy to the rules that govern things in possession. We argue that the law can recognise a control-based relative title to digital files, backed by a remedy for return or damages in case of third-party interference. Doing so can protect each person's control of their digital files, which serve as containers of valuable personal and commercial information. Yet it would also impact third parties, who would become subject to a duty of non-interference with digital files and potential liability for damages under the torts of trespass and conversion. Nonetheless, English law can also apply existing rules on freedom of contract, vicarious possession, abandonment, and involuntary bailment to digital files by analogy. This can help the law achieve an appropriate balance between the competing interests in digital files.

title: Governing AI: Leading Responsible Innovation
affiliations: Bentley University

detail.title: Governing AI: Leading Responsible Innovation
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has moved from research labs into everyday business operations, government services, and consumer products. This rapid adoption brings tremendous benefits but also significant risks. AI systems can discriminate against protected groups, invade privacy, make consequential errors, and concentrate power in ways that harm individuals and society. AI governance exists to help organizations capture the benefits of AI while managing these risks responsibly. This chapter establishes the foundational knowledge every AI governance professional needs. We begin by understanding what AI actually is and why it presents unique governance challenges. We then explore the principles that guide responsible AI development and deployment. Finally, we examine how organizations can establish governance structures, roles, and policies to manage AI effectively.

title: ERP Integration as a Strategic Capability: The Role of National Innovation Ecosystems in Europe

detail.title: ERP Integration as a Strategic Capability: The Role of National Innovation Ecosystems in Europe
detail.abstract: The current research aims to examine the reasons behind the higher ERP system integration in some European countries compared to others. This research conceptualizes ERP system integration not merely as a technological phenomenon but also as a strategic organizational capability. This research is based on the existing literature on Strategic Information Systems, digital transformation, and IT-Business alignment. This research aims to explore the impact of the external innovation ecosystem on ERP system diffusion and assimilation. This research utilizes a mixed research method that combines panel data analysis with machine learning algorithms and cluster analysis. This research utilizes panel data analysis by combining the ERP system integration data from the EUROSTAT database with the European Innovation Scoreboard. This research identifies that countries with higher innovation ecosystem maturity exhibit higher ERP system integration. This research also identifies different patterns of ERP system integration in various clusters of countries. This research has managerial implications that highlight the strategic importance of ERP system integration. This research also has implications for policymakers that highlight the importance of investing in the innovation ecosystem. This research contributes to the existing literature on Strategic Information Systems by combining macro-level data analysis with strategic insights on ERP system integration.

detail.title: From Routine to Revolutionary: The Impact of AI on Business

detail.abstract: The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed the way businesses operate across industries, ushering in a paradigm shift from traditional habits to cutting-edge digital practices. This article discusses the integration of AI with business and financial technology (FinTech), focusing on its use in streamlining efficiency, decision-making, customer experiences, and risk management. Major AI technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and robotics are being evaluated for their revolutionary impact. The study identifies both the benefits and drawbacks of using AI, including skill gaps, compatibility, ethics, privacy, and customer trust. Drawing on recent literature and practice, the paper explains how AI-enabled automation and data analytics help businesses gain a competitive advantage and achieve long-term growth. However, it warns that without proper governance, training, and ethical controls, AI can perpetuate bias and jeopardise data security. The study concludes that when used responsibly and inclusively, AI has the potential to drive innovation and economic empowerment, particularly in the FinTech industry.

title: Hide to Gain Visibility: Inducing Collaboration through Strategic Contract Unobservability
affiliations: , The University of Texas at Dallas, Jindal School of Management, University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management and Wuhan University - School of Economics and Management

detail.title: Hide to Gain Visibility: Inducing Collaboration through Strategic Contract Unobservability
detail.abstract: Information technology (IT)-enabled collaboration can substantially improve information sharing and coordination in supply chains, yet such collaboration is often hindered by organizational frictions. Even when information sharing would increase total supply chain surplus, downstream retailers possessing private demand information are typically reluctant to disclose it to upstream manufacturers, due to concerns about losing informational advantage or the information leaking to competitors. Consistent with empirical evidence, voluntary information sharing rarely occurs without explicit financial incentives. We show that contract visibilitywhether contracts between retailers and manufacturers are publicly observable or private-plays a critical role in shaping information-sharing incentives. When contracts are observable, retailers are unwilling to share information, resulting in a Prisoners' Dilemma. In contrast, when contracts are unobservable, retailers may voluntarily share demand information, particularly when retail competition is intense and demand signals are noisy. Contract unobservability thus emerges as a strategic instrument through which manufacturers can induce information sharing. Importantly, when information sharing is induced by unobservable contracts, the resulting outcomes can benefit not only manufacturers but also retailers, consumers, and overall social welfare. The underlying mechanism is that contract unobservability simultaneously limits the manufacturer's ability to engage in opportunistic behavior and mitigates the information-leakage effect that discourages disclosure. As a result, supply chain collaboration depends on the tradeoff between the value of contract observability and the value of information. These findings further suggest that policies mandating contract transparency, while intended to promote fairness, may inadvertently reduce efficiency by discouraging welfare-enhancing information sharing.

title: Inside Digital Heists: Cyber Fraud, Systemic Gaps, and the Fight for Accountability in India and Malaysia
affiliations: Supreme Court of India

detail.title: Inside Digital Heists: Cyber Fraud, Systemic Gaps, and the Fight for Accountability in India and Malaysia
detail.abstract: Cyber fraud is a fast-growing global threat that is reshaping security and trust in the digital world. As individuals and businesses around the world increasingly rely on digital platforms for communication, finance, and daily activities, cybercriminals are exploiting vulnerabilities to launch sophisticated attacks. From phishing scams in the United States to identity theft in India, ransomware in the United Kingdom, and financial fraud in China and Brazil, cyber fraud knows no borders. Notable cases, such as the 2017 WannaCry ransomware attack that affected over 150 countries, the Plus Token Ponzi scheme in China, the Facebook data breach in the UK, and the Nigerian email scam that stole millions globally, illustrate the extensive reach and impact of cyber fraud. This paper explores the various types of cyber fraud, phishing, identity theft, financial fraud, ransomware, and more through case studies from countries such as Australia, South Africa, Germany, and Japan. It examines the global response, including legal frameworks like the EU's GDPR, technological innovations like blockchain and AI, and international initiatives like INTERPOL's cybercrime efforts. Despite significant progress, challenges persist, particularly in jurisdictional issues, rapid technological advancements, and privacy concerns. This research highlights the need for a unified, global response to cyber fraud, emphasizing cooperation across borders to protect users and economies from this ever-evolving threat.

title: AI Data Readiness Moving to a Unified, Real-Time Information Fabric
affiliations: Independent, Independent and Independent

detail.title: AI Data Readiness Moving to a Unified, Real-Time Information Fabric
detail.abstract:
This paper is written for enterprise data, integration and technology leaders, any other executives responsible for driving AI and data-driven transformation and digital platform modernization. As organizations advance toward intelligent, context-aware systems powered by AI and increased use of the MCP, the pressure on the data foundation for AI has never been greater. BI, Advanced Analytics, and Agentic AI all depend on consistent, real-time, and trustworthy data. Yet, most enterprises still struggle with fragmented integration landscapes, delayed pipelines, and duplicated business logic that slow insight generation and limit AI effectiveness. The path forward lies in reimagining data integration, not just as a technical necessity for Analytics, but as the cornerstone of AI readiness, to ensure that every application, dashboard, and agent can access the same governed, high-quality information at the moment it is needed.

In this new reality, over many years enterprises have built two parallel data worlds:
The Integration World: initially powered by ESBs and message queues, and more recently by micro-services and REST APIs with point-to-point integrations that connect and drive applications.
The Analytics World: built around data warehouses, data lakes, and BI systems that support reporting, planning, and insights.

The result has often been duplicated logic, divergent definitions, and delayed insights. These parallel worlds created a fundamental split between acting on data as it was created (“Data in Motion”) and analyzing it after storage (“Data in Rest”). At the same time, in Gartner’s Data Management Hype Cycle for 2025, “AI-Ready Data” is identified as a fast mover and at the top of the Peak of Inflated Expectation. 

This leaves us with a fundamental question: how do we move forward from here?
This paper explains how to weave integration and analytics into a single, metadata-driven, event-centric fabric that delivers trusted, real-time information for business applications, analytical dashboards, and AI agents alike. 

This fabric exposes data from underlying sub-domains and data platforms through a common event broker and provides a unified consumption layer, often via a federated GraphQL Gateway, to ensure data is accessible when needed. The core shift is from a model that primarily values Data in Rest to one that harnesses the power of Data in Motion through a modern integration layer. This paper will also clarify what “graph” means in practice, how Change Data Capture (CDC) and event-driven architecture (EDA) work together, how to handle write-back, and most importantly how to ensure a single set of business logic is implemented once and reused everywhere.

The destination is a unified information landscape: event-driven, graph-aware, governed by active metadata and data contracts, implemented on modern platforms (e.g., Microsoft Azure/Fabric, Databricks, Snowflake, and Open-Source components), and inherently ready for AI.

title: User Perceptions of Misgendering Algorithms
affiliations: Leiden University, University of Baleares Islands, Leiden University, Leiden University - Center for Law in the Information Society, Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Leiden University - Center for Law in the Information Society, Leiden University Leiden Law School, Leiden University Leiden Law School and Leiden University - Center for Law and Digital Technologies

detail.title: User Perceptions of Misgendering Algorithms
detail.abstract: Gender classification systems (GCSs) on social media platforms, such as X (formerly Twitter), infer users' gender for targeted advertising and personalization. However, these systems rely on binary classifications that fail to capture gender diversity, often leading to misclassification (i.e. misgendering). This study is a comprehensive analysis of algorithmic misgendering and its impact on user perceptions through a large-scale online global survey (N = 1523). In the first stage, we assess the prevalence of misgendering on X by analyzing the accuracy of inferred gender classifications. Our findings reveal that women and LGBTQ+ users are disproportionately misclassified, which highlights structural biases in gender inference systems. In the second stage, given that the emotional and social consequences of algorithmic gender inference remain underexplored, we examine how users perceive and respond to misgendering. Using ordinal logistic regression models, we find that individuals who experience misgendering report significantly more aversion to X's gender policies. Furthermore, increased platform engagement is linked to stronger opinions on gender inference, reducing neutrality toward these systems. Beyond these findings, our study also reveals how opaque gender classification is, as many users struggle to locate, understand, or challenge their inferred gender within X's interface. This lack of transparency raises concerns about agency, algorithmic literacy, data protection, and fairness. Based on our work, we suggest regulatory measures to ensure greater transparency and user control over gender classification, contributing to ongoing debates on algorithmic discrimination and inclusive AI governance on current and future social media platforms.

title: From the Garden of Gartner to the Inevitable Implosion of LLM Credentialism: A Comprehensive Analysis of Pseudo -Technical Labor Markets, Credential Inflation, and the Coming Collapse
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: From the Garden of Gartner to the Inevitable Implosion of LLM Credentialism: A Comprehensive Analysis of Pseudo -Technical Labor Markets, Credential Inflation, and the Coming Collapse

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract:
The LLM labor market has produced a proliferation of roles branded as technical—prompt engineer, LLM agent designer, RLHF annotator, LLM operations specialist—that lack the engineering foundations their titles suggest. This paper documents the phenomenon and projects its collapse. A preliminary terminological note frames the analysis: all so-called "artificial intelligence" systems—machine learning models, neural networks, large language models—are human-engineered artifacts, designed, built, trained, and maintained by teams of STEM professionals. There is nothing "artificial" about their creation; the term obscures that LLMs are purposeful human constructs. The popular conflation of "AI" with "LLM" reflects widespread misunderstanding that credential marketing exploits.

Part I presents a comprehensive taxonomy of more than fifty pseudo-technical roles that have emerged since the crowdsourcing platforms of the early 2000s, through the data analytics boom of the 2010s, to the prompt engineering explosion and agentic wave of 2022-2026. Drawing on Randall Collins's credential inflation theory and Michael Spence's signaling theory, the paper analyzes the 'engineering veneer' pattern—the systematic application of engineering terminology to non-engineering work—and maps the credential provider ecosystem monetizing each technology wave.

Part II analyzes six market forces driving what this analysis projects as a structural correction: mass tech layoffs (429,608 in 2023), entry-level hiring collapse (25% decline at major firms), direct automation of interim human tasks, credential oversupply, title deflation, and regulatory shifts. A four-phase implosion model projects the timeline from denial (2023-2024, complete) through recognition (2024-2025, underway), contraction (2025-2027, emerging), and normalization (2027-2030, projected).

Part III engages six counterarguments—skills-based hiring, genuine sectoral demand, successful credential programs, human-LLM collaboration, regulatory demand, and historical precedent—and demonstrates why none rescues the broader credential economy. Policy implications are developed for workers, educators, employers, and policymakers.

The central finding: the pseudo-technical roles created during the AI hype cycle are scaffolding—temporary infrastructure that becomes unnecessary as LLM systems mature. What persists is structural: genuine engineering grounded in STEM, domain expertise that LLMs cannot replicate, and human-facing roles requiring relationships machines cannot replace. The implosion is not disaster but normalization—the recognition that LLM skills will become baseline literacy, not specialist identity, and that credential shortcuts cannot substitute for genuine expertise.

title: Science for Robot Policy Advancing Robotics Policy Through the EU Science for Policy Approach
affiliations: Leiden University, , Universiteit Leiden, eLaw, University of Baleares Islands, Leiden University - Leiden Law School and Leiden University - Center for Law and Digital Technologies

detail.title: Science for Robot Policy Advancing Robotics Policy Through the EU Science for Policy Approach

publicationDetails.detailsText: Technological Forecasting and Social Change, volume 218, 2025[10.1016/j.techfore.2025.124202]

detail.abstract: The rapid advancement of service robotics has outpaced regulatory frameworks, leading to gaps and inconsistencies that hinder effective governance. While evidence-based policymaking is well-established in health and consumer protection fields, robotics regulation remains fragmented and reactive. This paper proposes Science for Robot Policy, a structured, evidence-driven model that bridges the disconnect between robotics innovation and regulatory adaptation. Using a Constructive Research Approach, the model integrates scientific experimentation, stakeholder engagement, and knowledge brokering to generate policy-relevant data and transform it into actionable regulatory insights. The model follows a five-step process, beginning with risk identification and prioritization, followed by controlled experimentation in simulators, testing zones, living labs, and real-world markets. The ambition is that insights generated are then translated into policy-relevant information and further refined into knowledge for policymakers, ensuring that empirical evidence informs that robotics regulation is dynamic, anticipatory, and informed. This approach contributes to ongoing discussions on science-for-policy methodologies and fosters iterative regulatory refinement in service robotics. If successful, such a model could allow policymakers to address emerging risks proactively, reduce regulatory uncertainty, enhance user safety, and promote responsible robotics innovation by embedding scientific insights into the policy cycle.

title: Privacy Considerations for Socially Assistive Robots
affiliations: Leiden University, Leiden University - Center for Law in the Information Society and Leiden University - Center for Law and Digital Technologies

detail.title: Privacy Considerations for Socially Assistive Robots

publicationDetails.detailsText: In: Barfield, W., Weng, Y.H., Pagallo, U. (eds.) The Cambridge Handbook of the Law, Policy, and Regulation for Human-Robot Interaction. Cambridge University Press, p. 573-590.

detail.abstract: The integration of assisted living technologies in the home is rapidly accelerating. As socially assistive robots (SARs) often operate in the private sphere of life, sometimes in symbiotic relations with the people they assist, they may give rise to privacy concerns. This chapter investigates the potential privacy and data protection issues arising from the increasing deployment of assisted living technologies (AAL) in general and SARs in particular. It addresses privacy concerns related to human-robot interactions, including conversational interfaces, audio-and video-based assistive technologies, and analyzes them within the European context. Since the wide range of privacy concerns resulting from using SARs raises particular challenges for the design process, this article zooms in on the Privacy by Design concept introduced in the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Since communication and interaction with robots in therapeutic and care contexts impact data protection, these privacy concerns pose challenges that must be considered in a life cycle starting during the robot design and finalizing the implementation in care settings, including home care.

title: Agency, Tools, and Authorship in the Age of Large Language Models: A Demonstration and Analysis

keywords: Condition 1: The Human Authorship Doctrine: Burrow-Giles Lithographic Co

detail.abstract: This paper examines the nature of human authorship in an era of sophisticated large language model systems. Through a designed experiment in AI-assisted composition, it demonstrates that LLMs function as tools extending human cognitive reach rather than as autonomous creators capable of independent authorship. The study presents twelve mini-essays generated through human-LLM collaboration across diverse domains — law, physics, literary criticism, cultural anthropology, historical linguistics, structural engineering, fine arts, urban planning, cellular biology, cosmology, and philosophy — to illustrate that authorship resides in the human mind that conceives, directs, constrains, evaluates, and integrates expressive output. Drawing on U.S. copyright doctrine, including landmark Supreme Court and appellate decisions establishing the human authorship requirement, as well as U.S. Copyright Office guidance on AI-generated works, the paper establishes that legal authorship requires human creative control and original intellectual conception. Philosophically, it argues that authorship is grounded in intentionality, meaning-making, and responsibility — capacities that LLMs simulate but do not possess. Engaging counterarguments from extended-cognition theory, emergent-intentionality claims, edge cases of thin human control, and the case for AI as co-author, the paper proposes the Houze/Maestro Model, a portable authorship protocol for AI-era scholarship that defines roles, disclosure elements, acceptable practices, an epistemic checklist for human authors, and implementation guidance for institutions. The paper's methodology itself enacts the model it proposes: initial essays were generated by Microsoft Copilot, the analytical framework was developed through iterative dialogue with Claude Opus 4.5, and successive drafts were submitted for LLM peer review by multiple systems, with all revisions accepted or rejected by the human author. Handwritten pre-interaction notes are presented as Feistian artifacts — documentary evidence of human-originated conceptual architecture preceding any LLM engagement. The paper concludes that academia's reluctance to embrace LLMs as legitimate scholarly tools reflects, in significant part, cultural lag rather than conceptual rigor, while acknowledging that measured institutional caution serves legitimate pedagogical and integrity interests.

title: Best Arm Identification with LLM Judges and Limited Human Audits
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), City University of Hong Kong, City University of Hong Kong and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - School of Engineering

detail.title: Best Arm Identification with LLM Judges and Limited Human Audits

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest statement
declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethics to declare

detail.abstract: We study fixed-confidence best-arm identification (BAI) where a cheap but potentially biased proxy (e.g., LLM judge) is available for every sample, while an expensive ground-truth label can only be acquired selectively when using a human for auditing. Unlike classical multi-fidelity BAI, the proxy is biased (arm-and context-dependent) and ground truth is selectively observed. Consequently, standard multi-fidelity methods can mis-select the best arm, and uniform auditing, though accurate, wastes scarce resources and is inefficient. We prove that without bias correction and propensity adjustment, mis-selection probability may not vanish (even with unlimited proxy data). We then develop an estimator for the mean of each arm that combines proxy scores with inverse-propensity-weighted residuals and form anytime-valid confidence sequences for that estimator. Based on the estimator and confidence sequence, we propose an algorithm that adaptively selects and audits arms. The algorithm concentrates audits on unreliable contexts and close arms and we prove that a plug-in Neyman rule achieves near-oracle audit efficiency. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical guarantees and demonstrate the superior empirical performance of the proposed algorithm.

detail.abstract: This study looks at how well fiscal, monetary, and regulatory policies compare in promoting economic stability and growth. By focusing on the effect of recent reforms at the national and international level, the research assesses the lag and effectiveness of different intervention strategies. Employing a multi-dimensional analytical framework, it evaluates the interplay between regulatory change, fiscal constraints, and monetary adjustment to reduce economic volatility.

title: Vietnam's Involvement in the Halal Food Industry: Opportunities and Challenges for ASEAN Integration

detail.title: Vietnam's Involvement in the Halal Food Industry: Opportunities and Challenges for ASEAN Integration
detail.abstract: This paper posits that Vietnam's entry into the global Halal market is not merely an economic diversification strategy but a geopolitical imperative for ASEAN integration. While Vietnam dominates global export indices for coffee and rice, it suffers from a deficit of "ethical capital"-the trust mechanisms required to penetrate Muslim-majority markets. The establishment of the National Halal Certification Authority (HALCERT) via Decision No. 689/QĐ-TĐC represents a critical institutional pivot from ad-hoc certification to stateguaranteed compliance. However, the analysis reveals that this domestic centralization is insufficient against the external reality of regulatory fragmentation. The "Standardization Nightmare"-specifically the dissonance between Malaysia's JAKIM and Indonesia's BPJPH standards-serves as a potent non-tariff barrier. The paper argues that without bilateral Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs), Vietnam's infrastructural investments will yield suboptimal returns.

title: The Knowable Future: Mapping the Decay of Past-Future Mutual Information Across Forecast Horizons

detail.title: The Knowable Future: Mapping the Decay of Past-Future Mutual Information Across Forecast Horizons
detail.abstract: Forecasting fails not because models are weak, but because effort is wasted on series whose futures are fundamentally unknowable. We propose a pre-modelling diagnostic framework that assesses horizon-specific forecastability before model selection begins, enabling practitioners to allocate effort where it can yield returns. We operationalise forecastability as auto-mutual information (AMI) at lag h, measuring the reduction in uncertainty about future values provided by the past. Using a k-nearest-neighbour estimator on training data only, we validate AMI against realised out-of-sample error (sMAPE) across 1,350 M4 series spanning six frequencies, with Seasonal Naïve, ETS, and N-BEATS as probe models under a rolling-origin protocol. The central finding is that the AMI-sMAPE relationship is strongly frequency-conditional. For Weekly, Hourly, Quarterly, and Yearly series, AMI exhibits consistent negative rank association with realised error (Spearman ρ ranging from-0.52 to-0.66 for higher-capacity probes), supporting its use as a triage signal. Monthly shows moderate association; Daily exhibits weaker discrimination despite measurable dependence. Across all frequencies, median forecast error decreases monotonically from low to high AMI terciles, confirming decision-relevant separation. These results establish AMI as a practical screening tool for forecasting portfolios: identifying series where sophisticated modelling is warranted, where baselines suffice, and where effort should shift from accuracy improvement to robust decision design.

title: Revisiting the Idiosyncratic Volatility Puzzle in China: Evidence from Deep Learning Models
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) - School of Finance, Central University of Finance and Economics, Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) - School of Finance and School of Finance, Central University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Revisiting the Idiosyncratic Volatility Puzzle in China: Evidence from Deep Learning Models
detail.abstract: This paper revisits the idiosyncratic volatility (IVOL) puzzle in the Chinese stock market using a comparative analysis of alternative IVOL forecasting models. We show that deep learning approaches, such as the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT), and conventional time-series models like ARMA(1,1) substantially outperform the martingale benchmark in predictive accuracy. The IVOL puzzle proves fragile for total returns: while the Martingale forecast produces a significant negative relationship between IVOL and returns, this effect disappears under TFT-based forecasts in Fama-French regressions and is fully absorbed by the CH-4 factor model. Forecast error decomposition reveals that Martingale overestimation induces spurious negative correlations. Further decomposing returns show negative IVOL exposure overnight but positive intraday compensation, which largely offset in aggregate. The TFT model more accurately captures the true intraday risk premium, explaining the lack of robustness in the IVOL puzzle.

title: Capacity Blindness in Rural Governance: Regional Commissions and the Limits of Template-Based Technical Assistance

detail.title: Capacity Blindness in Rural Governance: Regional Commissions and the Limits of Template-Based Technical Assistance
detail.abstract:
Regional planning commissions play a central role in providing technical assistance to small municipalities that lack professional administrative capacity. In theory, these intergovernmental intermediaries are intended to diagnose local needs and tailor governance solutions accordingly. In practice, however, technical assistance frequently degenerates into the distribution of standardized ordinances and model policies that presume administrative capacities rural towns do not possess.

This paper examines the Southwest Georgia Regional Commission as an illustrative case of a broader institutional failure affecting rural municipal governance. Using a county-by-county audit of municipal populations and documentary analysis of an administrative ordinance adopted by a small town, the paper demonstrates a persistent mismatch between governance frameworks supplied and local capacity to administer them. Approximately 61 percent of municipalities in the region have fewer than 1,000 residents, and approximately 83 percent have fewer than 5,000 residents, yet the technical assistance provided often reflects assumptions appropriate only to much larger jurisdictions.

The paper argues that template-based assistance, absent discovery-based capacity assessment, creates compliance risk rather than institutional resilience. It concludes by proposing a tiered model of governance assistance calibrated explicitly to municipal size, staffing, and administrative feasibility.

title: PPI-SVRG: Unifying Prediction-Powered Inference and Variance Reduction for Semi-Supervised Optimization
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Washington University in St. Louis, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - School of Engineering and Purdue University

detail.title: PPI-SVRG: Unifying Prediction-Powered Inference and Variance Reduction for Semi-Supervised Optimization
detail.abstract: We study semi-supervised stochastic optimization when labeled data is scarce but predictions from pretrained models are available. PPI and SVRG both reduce variance through control variates-PPI uses predictions, SVRG uses reference gradients. We show they are mathematically equivalent and develop PPI-SVRG, which combines both. Our convergence bound decomposes into the standard SVRG rate plus an error floor from prediction uncertainty. The rate depends only on loss geometry; predictions affect only the neighborhood size. When predictions are perfect, we recover SVRG exactly. When predictions degrade, convergence remains stable but reaches a larger neighborhood. Experiments confirm the theory: PPI-SVRG reduces MSE by 43-52% under label scarcity on mean estimation benchmarks and improves test accuracy by 2.7-2.9 percentage points on MNIST with only 10% labeled data.

title: Green Sukuk Product Development: The Potential for Sustainable Infrastructure Financing in the Sharia Capital Market
affiliations: Bung Karno University

detail.title: Green Sukuk Product Development: The Potential for Sustainable Infrastructure Financing in the Sharia Capital Market
detail.abstract: This paper thoroughly examines the development of Green Sukuk products as sustainable financing instruments in the Islamic capital market, focusing on their potential to fund green infrastructure in Indonesia. Through literature analysis, empirical data, and case studies, this research finds that Green Sukuk not only comply with Sharia principles but also attract global investors to support the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The main findings indicate a 15% annual growth in the green sukuk market, with infrastructure financing potential reaching up to IDR 500 trillion. Recommendations include regulatory harmonization and product innovation to address challenges such as greenwashing. This paper employs a mixed methodology, including literature review and secondary data analysis, to ensure the validity of the findings.

title: The Mechanics of Endogenous Diffusion: A Tractable Analytical Framework

contentType.other: Research paper submitted to a journal

detail.abstract: This note develops a growth model in which the diffusion of capital goods is endogenized through the interaction between monopolistic suppliers and a final-goods sector. We introduce a distinction between private and social returns to adoption: while individual firms operate under constant or diminishing returns-ensuring a stable micro-foundation for profit maximization-aggregate production exhibits increasing returns driven by system-wide diffusion complementarities and adoption externalities. The model derives a closed-form solution for the long-run growth rate, which is shown to depend on the user cost of capital and the strength of these aggregate complementarities. Specifically, we find that lower financing costs and declining relative prices for capital goods accelerate diffusion. By explicitly modeling the transition from microlevel adoption to macro-level increasing returns, this framework provides a structural mechanism explaining how economies sustain growth through the propagation of innovations, complementing standard R&D-based approaches.

detail.abstract: While Six Sigma has matured around tools for preventing defects in process control there has not been enough development around auditing frameworks, we can use to verify readiness, governance, trustworthiness, and transparency. Building from Lean Six Sigma this paper proposes governance auditing requirements as derived from organizational readiness literature, ISO 9001 process integrity controls, ISO 26000 guidance on social responsibility, and ISO 37001 guidance on anti-bribery. Key insights synthesized here argue for readiness auditing as a closed-loop control system encapsulated within the Define–Measure–Analyze–Improve-Control–Reflect (DMAIC-R) cycle. Governance auditing overlays enable organizations to design systems thinking audits across each phase of the operational life cycle. Introducing concepts like governance audits, ethical defect auditing, communication readiness audits, and reflective audit controls this working paper lays conceptual groundwork for discussing how to measure and control readiness as an operating system.

detail.abstract: The United Kingdom has adopted a principles-based, sector-led approach to artificial intelligence (AI) governance, with sector regulators responsible for early oversight and escalation. While this architecture is designed to balance innovation and risk management, it has largely been developed under relatively stable conditions. Its behaviour under early phase incident uncertainty, before escalation thresholds can be confidently applied and where public guidance only partially specifies how authority and escalation operate across remits, has not been directly stress-tested. This paper presents a qualitative, desk-based governance stress test examining how UK AI governance arrangements behave under severe but plausible conditions of uncertainty. Rather than assessing technical systems or cyber operations, the analysis focuses on first-order governance functions: authority and accountability, information and situational awareness, escalation and mobilisation, and institutional capacity and adaptation. Using a scenario-based failure mode logic adapted from safety-critical domains and drawing on publicly available mandates, guidance and observable practice, the paper identifies recurring system-level governance failure modes which arise from structural features of governance design rather than isolated organisational error. The findings are diagnostic in nature, aiming to surface early phase governance fragilities in the partially specified interval before formal crisis mechanisms are activated, rather than to prescribe reform.

detail.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into legal services has generated significant debate regarding trust, accountability, fairness, and ethical responsibility. This study examines public perceptions of AI-assisted legal representation through a survey-based analysis conducted with 147 participants. The research explores attitudes toward the use of artificial intelligence across different stages of legal processes, ranging from supportive and low-risk functions to decision-influencing applications. The findings reveal a notably divided public opinion, with attitudes often approaching an even balance between acceptance and skepticism. However, despite this apparent equilibrium, the results indicate that positive perceptions toward AI-assisted legal services are comparatively strong given the novelty of artificial intelligence in the legal domain. The emergence of such a level of public trust at an early stage of technological integration suggests a rapid shift in societal attitudes toward AI-supported legal practice. Acceptance increases significantly when artificial intelligence is framed as a supportive tool operating under human oversight, while concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, accountability, and the absence of human judgment continue to shape public hesitation. Beyond measuring public attitudes, the study aims to provide guidance for legal professionals by identifying societal trust thresholds and expectations surrounding AI use in legal representation. In this regard, the findings offer an informative framework for lawyers seeking to integrate artificial intelligence into their professional activities while maintaining ethical standards, transparency, and public confidence.

detail.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to present the IAM Six Sigma for Readiness Framework, which integrates ethical readiness metrics into Lean Six Sigma continuous improvement initiatives. Lean Six Sigma has been largely focused on reducing errors and inefficiencies. It stands to reason that fewer governance lapses, built-in trust, and transparency can also be realized as a result of improved Lean Six Sigma initiatives. However, these types of metrics have not been fully quantified and integrated into Lean Six Sigma deployment plans. The author then discusses how the IAM Six Sigma for Readiness Framework incorporates constructs from established readiness literature as well as international standards such as ISO 9001, ISO 26000, and ISO 37001 into a revised six-phase DMAIC cycle (Define-Measure-Analyze-Improve-Control-Reflect) to assess and target readiness and ethical performance. detail.abstract: The Domain Name System (DNS) is a foundational component of Internet infrastructure, responsible for translating human-readable domain names into numerical network addresses. While the DNS protocol itself has remained largely stable, the operational model governing authoritative DNS has shifted significantly with the rise of managed DNS services. Managed DNS refers to the outsourcing of authoritative DNS hosting, operation, and security to specialized third-party providers operating globally distributed infrastructures. This paper presents a conceptual and analytical review of managed DNS, examining its architectural foundations, performance characteristics, security implications, and economic trade-offs relative to self-managed DNS models. Drawing on industry practices and DNS protocol fundamentals, the study analyzes how managed DNS transforms DNS from a static resolution mechanism into a programmable control layer for availability, resilience, and traffic management.

title: MM, Coase, and Corporate Finance
affiliations: University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business - Finance and Business Economics Department and University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: MM, Coase, and Corporate Finance
detail.abstract: Despite cosmetic similarities, the Modigliani-Miller and Coase Theorems provide conceptually distinct insights for corporate finance theory, with neither theorem a special case of the other. Coase's main lesson is the existence of opportunity-cost pressure toward allocative efficiency, which in a corporate finance context means pressure to increase firm value. Such pressure plays no role in the MM Theorem, which indicates that the firm's choice of financial policy is indeterminate (because all choices are equally valuable) and whose main lesson is that investment policy is the foundational driver of firm value.

detail.abstract: This paper examines architectural trade-offs in autonomous driving chip design through the lens of Tesla-style vision-only Full Self-Driving (FSD) systems versus sensor-fusion robotaxi stacks. Focusing on memory hierarchy behavior, cache capacity, and DRAM technology choices (LPDDR versus HBM), the study investigates how end-to-end (E2E) architectures shape both technical performance and competitive dynamics among US, Chinese, and Taiwanese semiconductor suppliers. title: Entropy Alignment: A Framework for Governing Randomness in AI-Enabled Enterprise Systems

detail.title: Entropy Alignment: A Framework for Governing Randomness in AI-Enabled Enterprise Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal, financial, or commercial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest with respect to the research, authorship, or publication of this work.

detail.abstract:
As artificial intelligence systems move from experimental deployments into operational and decision-critical enterprise environments, organizations struggle to balance automation, predictability, creativity, and trust. Existing AI governance frameworks emphasize ethics, transparency, and risk mitigation, yet often fail to provide a unifying technical principle that explains how and where uncertainty should be permitted within intelligent systems.

This paper introduces Entropy Alignment, a systems-level framework that treats entropy as the controlled application of randomness across different layers of AI-enabled enterprise systems. Drawing from thermodynamics, information theory, cryptography, cybernetics, and modern machine learning, we argue that effective AI modernization is not a question of maximizing or minimizing intelligence, but of intentionally placing randomness according to business intent.

We show that automation corresponds to near-zero entropy, adaptive intelligence requires bounded entropy, and ungoverned systems drift toward pathological high-entropy behaviors such as hallucination and instability. By framing AI behavior through entropy profiles rather than model classes or vendor capabilities, organizations gain a practical mechanism for aligning predictability, innovation, and trust. The framework offers actionable guidance for enterprise AI governance, system design, and risk containment.

title: A Cybernetic Invariant Across Biological, Digital, and Organizational Intelligence

detail.title: A Cybernetic Invariant Across Biological, Digital, and Organizational Intelligence

detail.abstract:
Across biological brains, large-scale digital networks, and modern artificial intelligence systems, intelligence exhibits a recurring structural pattern: adaptive behavior emerges not from globally synchronized computation, but from selectively propagated signals operating within constrained, conditionally activated subspaces. This paper proposes a unifying cybernetic invariant governing intelligent systems operating under resource, energy, bandwidth, latency, and trust constraints.

Drawing from classical cybernetics, computational neuroscience, network theory, organizational systems, and contemporary transformer architectures, we argue that locality, conditional activation, feedback control, and bounded propagation are necessary conditions for scalable intelligence, rather than implementation preferences or architectural accidents. We formalize this invariant as a constraint-driven control principle, derive quantitative implications using control-theoretic and information-theoretic bounds, and demonstrate its manifestation across biological neural systems, internet-scale networks, modern AI models, and organizational execution architectures.

The framework yields falsifiable predictions regarding system stability, modularity, and scaling behavior, with direct implications for AI governance, enterprise control systems, and the design of resilient intelligent infrastructures. Rather than proposing a new algorithm or mechanism, this work offers a unifying explanatory framework that clarifies why intelligent systems consistently converge on sparse activation, modular organization, and gated execution across substrates.

title: Vertical Restraints of Trade as Contractual Integration: A Synthesis of Relational Contracting Theory, Transaction-Cost Economics, and Organization Theory

detail.title: Vertical Restraints of Trade as Contractual Integration: A Synthesis of Relational Contracting Theory, Transaction-Cost Economics, and Organization Theory

detail.abstract:
The Supreme Court's oscillating treatment of nonprice vertical restraints under the antitrust laws has been widely discussed. Although the Court has not developed a coherent, workable model for analyzing the legality of vertical restraints, a consensus as to the economic nature and function of these restraints has emerged. The most recent major swing in the Court's position—the return of the Rule of Reason in Continental T.V., Inc. v. GTE Sylvania, Inc.—embraced the following economic syllogism for evaluating antitrust doctrines: (1) the goal of antitrust policy is the promotion of consumer welfare; (2) consumer welfare is advanced by economic efficiency; therefore, (3) antitrust policy should not interfere with business practices that increase economic efficiency. Primarily because the adopted standard of efficiency has been consumer welfare, economics provides the most useful tool for the analysis of antitrust doctrines. Economic analyses of business practices categorized as vertical restraints have concentrated on ad hoc theoretical rationalizations for their adoption by firms, as well as theoretical analyses of their effects on economic efficiency—the main theme being the identification of situations where profit maximization and increased economic efficiency coincide. There are, however, some areas of antitrust, such as vertical restrictions, in which the general framework of economics can be profitably supplemented by other disciplines. Economists, because their fundamental unit of analysis is the firm, have neglected the logical processes by which businessmen decide to adopt and implement business practices related to the internal organization and external relationships of the firm. This neglect is unfortunate because analysis of vertical restraints at a lower level of abstraction, i.e., within the firm, may lead to additional insights into their efficiency implications and, thus, to a correct antitrust policy. 

Organization theory, a branch of the management sciences concerned with the analysis of factors that affect the decisions of managers to implement various business practices, can be especially useful in reaching policy decisions since it provides an explicit and practical explanation of many business practices. Interfirm relationships that would be classified as vertical restraints under antitrust law are included among the various practices and strategies studied by organization theorists. The contributions of organization theory, however, have not been applied to a policy analysis of antitrust law. Given the Supreme Court's recently adopted paradigm for evaluating the legality of business practices, a consideration of the attributes of business practices, which have been analyzed, categorized, and developed by organization theorists, will provide additional tools for the analysis of antitrust questions. Both economics and organization theory can be used to capture subtleties associated with the type of long-term contracts that characterize most vertical restrictions. Moreover, a synthesis of the economic and organization theory approaches can be formulated through an expansion of the traditional analysis of contract law to include long-term relational contracting theories. 

This article attempts to synthesize into a general theoretical framework the contributions of these various disciplines—contract law theory, economics, and organization theory—and apply the framework to the specific issues surrounding the antitrust law of vertical restraints. This general-theory-to-specific-application approach serves to emphasize the point that vertical restraints are merely a category of generic business practices that may enhance economic efficiency through a partial suppression of market forces." The efficiency-enhancing aspects of these business practices indicate that a proper antitrust policy should incorporate a strong, yet rebuttable, presumption of their legality.

title: Patent Quality Versus Quantity in the Intangible Economy: A Cross-Industry Empirical Analysis of Innovation-Driven Market Valuation
affiliations: University of Liège - HEC-Liège, Management School of the University of Liège

detail.title: Patent Quality Versus Quantity in the Intangible Economy: A Cross-Industry Empirical Analysis of Innovation-Driven Market Valuation
detail.abstract: This study examines how patent portfolios relate to market capitalization in an economy where intangible assets account for roughly 90% of corporate value. Using a 10-year panel (2015-2024) of 40 public firms across technology, pharmaceutical, and consumer sectors, I estimate OLS, firm fixed-effects, and generalized estimating equation models within the Hall-Jaffe-Trajtenberg valuation framework to test whether citation-weighted patent quality outperforms raw patent quantity as a predictor of market value. Results show that citation elasticity (β₃ = 0.26-0.31, p < 0.01) is approximately 2-3× larger than the elasticity of patent productivity (β₂ = 0.06-0.12), indicating that patent quality is substantially more informative for valuation than simple counts. Technical founder-CEOs sustain about 22% higher R&D intensity and exhibit a positive interaction with citation quality, while geographic filing breadth serves as a cost-effective quality proxy: only 3.3% of Chinese patents are filed internationally versus more than 70% for advanced economies. Sector heterogeneity is pronounced, with the patent-value relationship strongest in pharmaceuticals (ρ ≈ 0.71), moderate in semiconductors, and weak and often statistically insignificant in consumer goods. Case studies of NVIDIA's decade-long CUDA investment, Intel's forgone AI platform bets, and a projected 2025-2030 pharmaceutical "patent cliff" illustrate the mechanisms by which technical leadership and AI-enabled drug discovery reshape the economic returns to patents. The findings imply that conventional patent metrics systematically mismeasure innovation value and suggest that investors, corporate strategists, and policy makers should overweight citation velocity and geographic breadth-rather than raw counts-when evaluating innovation-driven market value.

title: Priority Access for Ecosystem Seeding
affiliations: Zhongnan University of Economics and Law - School of Finance,  and University of Southern California Gould School of Law

detail.title: Priority Access for Ecosystem Seeding
detail.abstract: Leading technology providers often adopt ecosystem seeding-cultivating promising partners before commercial potential is fully realized-as a strategy to sustain dominance. Yet supply constraints-such as limited capacity in advanced semiconductor manufacturing-limit their ability to serve all potential customers (e.g., AI startups) and fully unleash the value of their technology edge. Programs such as Nvidia's Inception illustrate one response: engaging a broad pool of potential buyers and prioritizing access to scarce resources. This paper examines how such priority access mechanisms can better enable ecosystem seeding and improve long-run firm value and how they shape competition, supply-chain outcomes, and technological innovation. We study a two-period supply chain in which an incumbent sellers interacts with rival suppliers and forward-looking buyers under endogenous pricing and technology development decisions. The incumbent could grant priority access to selective buyers based on its assessment of buyers' prospect. Relative to price-based allocation, priority access is most valuable to the incumbent when the supply constraint is severe or when buyer switching costs are high. Surprisingly, the value of priority access does not necessarily increase with the incumbent's assessment quality. While priority access primarily benefits the incumbent, it can also raise rival profitability, improve supply-chain efficiency, and accelerate technology development. These benefits can be further enhanced through strategic information disclosure and multi-tiered prioritization. Our analysis reveals when priority access can serve as an effective strategic lever for supply-constrained technology leaders. They also inform debates about the competitive effects of such programs by highlighting conditions under which access prioritization generates positive spillovers beyond the incumbent. Finally, the findings offers practical guidance on the design and operationalization of priority access mechanisms.

title: Complexity Creep
affiliations: Indiana University Maurer School of Law (Bloomington)

detail.title: Complexity Creep
detail.abstract:
We use software to save time, and then we spend that time managing the software. This Article names the pattern: complexity creep – the gradual proliferation of features, options, updates, and incompatibilities that transforms functional software tools into drains on time and productivity. No one sets out to create it; complexity creep emerges from market forces and competitive dynamics that reward accumulation over efficiency.

The Article makes three contributions. Empirically, it presents the first systematic estimate of the costs of complexity creep, synthesizing industry surveys, government data, and natural experiments. Digital friction costs American workers roughly five to seven hours per week, amounting to hundreds of billions – likely over one trillion – dollars annually in lost time. This burden falls disproportionately on older workers and those with lower digital literacy, functioning as a regressive tax on time.

Conceptually, the Article frames complexity creep as a form of digital pollution: firms impose time costs they do not bear, users cannot evaluate complexity before purchase or escape it afterward, and markets reward feature accumulation rather than correcting for it. This is a classic externality – and like environmental pollution before the Clean Air Act, it will not self-correct. Legally, the Article demonstrates why contract, tort, consumer protection, and antitrust frameworks each fail to address it. Drawing on environmental law’s evolution from nuisance to statutory regulation, the Article develops a regulatory toolkit designed to internalize time costs. The toolkit includes complexity disclosures, symmetry requirements, impact statements, and interoperability mandates.

detail.abstract: Advanced technologies are widely promoted as tools for decarbonization across sectors such as manufacturing, logistics, and energy. However, evidence of their environmental impact remains mixed, with outcomes varying significantly between settings. This variability highlights the need to understand how national institutional contexts shape the implementation and effectiveness of these technologies. A comparative international business perspective is especially useful in uncovering why the same technology leads to different results between countries, revealing the role of regulatory environments, market dynamics, and organizational norms. This paper uses a problematizing review method to critically examine five types of assumptions found in current research: in-house, root metaphor, paradigm, ideology, and field assumptions. This paper analyzes these assumptions through diagnostic, prognostic, and motivational framings. The data for this review was drawn from a systematic search of the Web of Science and Scopus databases, supplemented by manual searches of high-ranking journals across multiple disciplines, resulting in a final sample of 64 relevant peer-reviewed articles. Our contribution includes exposing blind spots in existing literature, proposing a future research agenda, and encouraging a more contextsensitive, institutionally informed approach to technology and decarbonization in comparative international business.

detail.abstract: All researchers face pressure to demonstrate significance, but whether that pressure distorts findings may depend on how observable their analytic choices are. We examine this in clinical trials, where academic and industry sponsors face similar evidentiary benchmarks but differ in documentation practices and oversight contexts. Using p-value distributions from 10,596 completed randomized clinical trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, we test for threshold-driven distortions around p = 0.05. Academicsponsored trials exhibit an excess of primary-outcome p-values just below 0.05, while industry-sponsored trials show little or no such pattern; secondary outcomes show no comparable distortion for either sponsor type. Internal consistency checks between reported p-values and 95% confidence intervals replicate the same sponsor gap, and a validation exercise using p-values extracted from PubMed Central trial publications yields similar directional differences. The academic-industry gap persists after adjusting for trial characteristics, suggesting that organizational setting itself may matter. We examine the 2013 SPIRIT statement (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials), which standardized protocol documentation for clinical trials. Academic trials initiated after SPIRIT show weaker evidence of threshold-adjacent bunching than those initiated earlier, whereas trials initiated earlier but reported later show no comparable change-a pattern suggestive of protocol design and documentation as a relevant margin.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the November 2025 restructuring of the National Association of Social Workers (NASW) through the lens of organizational silence and governance accountability. The analysis documents a systematic pattern in which social workers who witnessed or experienced concerning institutional practices felt unable to speak publicly due to fear of professional retaliation. Drawing on direct communications with former staff, chapter leaders, and current members, the paper reveals how silence itself becomes evidence of power dynamics that contradict core social work values.

The restructuring eliminated fourteen state chapter executive director positions and consolidated governance authority at the national level. Financial analysis of IRS Form 990 filings demonstrates that this decision was not driven by fiscal emergency. Membership dues remained stable from 2021-2024, and the organization showed positive net income in three of the past four fiscal years. This reframes the restructuring as a governance choice rather than a financial necessity.

At least seven state chapters have taken formal institutional action challenging national leadership decisions, including votes of no confidence from Iowa, Texas, and Michigan chapters. These actions cite concerns about transparency, participatory decision-making, and adherence to the profession's Code of Ethics. The paper situates these governance failures within the broader phenomenon of clinical drift, arguing that centralized organizational structures mirror the profession's systematic retreat from macro practice and systems change.

The analysis reveals critical tensions between NASW's role as teacher of ethical practice and its own organizational behavior. When a professional association that trains social workers in transparency, accountability, and speaking truth to power operates through opacity and discourages dissent, it undermines the moral authority of the entire profession. The paper concludes with recommendations for governance reform grounded in social work's foundational commitment to participatory democracy and ethical stewardship.

title: Structural Analysis of Assembly Systems with Component Demand and Capacity Constraints
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - College of Business and University of British Columbia

detail.title: Structural Analysis of Assembly Systems with Component Demand and Capacity Constraints
detail.abstract: We study a multi-stage assembly inventory system in which demands arise for components in addition to the assembled product. Production at each stage is constrained by capacity. These features violate the inventory balance conditions that underpin classic decomposition-based analyses of assembly systems, rendering existing structural results inapplicable. We introduce an equivalent reformulation that converts component backlogging into a lost-sales representation, which induces a monotone ordering structure on echelon inventories. Our main theoretical result establishes that the dynamic cost-to-go functions of the reformulated system are $L^\natural$-convex. This discrete convexity property implies convexity and submodularity and yields economically meaningful monotone optimal policies and bounded sensitivity of decisions across stages. In particular, optimal ordering, assembly, and component allocation decisions are monotone in echelon inventory states and adjust in a structured manner in response to inventory perturbations. These results provide new structural insights for assembly systems with dual-use components and capacity limitations, extending classic assembly theory beyond balanced inventory regimes.

title: Balancing Occupational Health, Economy and Environment in Abandoned Industrial Building Reconstruction: A Multi-objective Optimization Perspective

detail.title: Balancing Occupational Health, Economy and Environment in Abandoned Industrial Building Reconstruction: A Multi-objective Optimization Perspective
detail.abstract: Adaptive reuse of abandoned industrial buildings is increasingly recognized as a strategic pathway for reducing lifecycle carbon emissions and supporting low-carbon urban energy transitions. However, renovation activities are often characterized by pronounced trade-offs among occupational health protection, economic feasibility, and environmental performance, particularly under conditions of confined spaces, residual pollutants, and high workforce density. Existing sustainability-oriented decision frameworks rarely quantify these interdependencies within a unified, scalable optimization structure. This study develops a transferable multi-objective decision framework to support low-carbon renovation planning for abandoned industrial buildings by simultaneously minimizing occupational health risk (H), project cost (C), and carbon emissions (E). A hierarchical evaluation system is established in which workforce density and pollutant diffusion are explicitly incorporated as key determinants of health risk. A constrained multi-objective optimization model is formulated subject to resource availability, workforce safety thresholds, and pollutant diffusion control. The Pareto-optimal solution space is explored using NSGA-III, and a comprehensive optimal solution is identified through the Entropy - TOPSIS method. The case study indicates that the proposed framework achieves balanced system-level improvements, reducing H, C, and E by 1.1%, 2.3%, and 5.1%, respectively, relative to the baseline scenario. Extreme single-objective solutions expose substantial trade-offs: a 1.6% reduction in occupational health risk results in increases of 19.8% in cost and 14.9% in carbon emissions, whereas low-cost and low-emission strategies lead to a 1.4–1.7% increase in health risk. The proposed framework provides quantitative evidence to support sustainability-oriented policy design, investment prioritization, and large-scale deployment of low-carbon regeneration strategies for industrial building stock.

detail.title: Supporting the Adoption of Research Partnerships in Spinal Cord Injury Research: An exploratory case study of a research centre
detail.abstract: BackgroundResearch coproduction may help to enhance the relevance, usefulness, and application of spinal cord injury (SCI) research. The Integrated Knowledge Translation (IKT) Guiding Principles were developed to support meaningful SCI research partnerships, yet limited evidence exists on how research institutions can support their adoption.PurposeThis study aimed to explore how coproduction is practiced and supported within a SCI research centre and to identify strategies for fostering principles-based research coproduction.MethodsThis exploratory retrospective case study was conducted at ICORD, a multidisciplinary SCI research centre located in Vancouver, British Columbia. Data sources included ten years of internal grant applications, a network analysis of research collaborations, and surveys and interviews with researchers, trainees, and partners. Grant applications were coded to assess coproduction characteristics and analyzed using descriptive statistics. Interviews and surveys were analyzed using the Theoretical Domains Framework and Behaviour Change Wheel to identify barriers, facilitators, and potential intervention strategies.ResultsOf the 160 internal grant applications, 28.8% included non-academic partners, and those projects were significantly less likely to be funded (p<0.001, Cramér’s V=0.278). Network analysis showed collaborations were largely siloed within academia. Survey and interview participants were interested in coproduction but cited limited skills, institutional support, and unclear expectations as barriers. Supportive leadership, mentorship, and visible examples were seen as key enablers. Across methods, participants called for capacity building, clearer guidance, dedicated funding, and changes to review processes to better support and value research partnerships.ConclusionsThis study provides a theory-informed analysis of coproduction within an academic research centre. Findings suggest that research institutions can play a critical role in enabling coproduction by embedding supportive structures, processes, and cultural shifts. These insights can inform efforts to advance more inclusive and impactful SCI research.

detail.abstract:
Organizations today face increasing expectations to ensure the effectiveness of their compliance programs. Regulatory guidance, including the Department of Justice’s Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs, emphasizes not only the existence of compliance structures but their ongoing effectiveness in preventing, detecting, and responding to misconduct. These expectations place boards of directors at the center of compliance oversight, even where boards may lack the expertise or information necessary to assess whether internal systems are functioning as intended. In response, organizations have turned to a growing market of outside compliance consultants to assist boards in evaluating speak-up mechanisms, investigation processes, compliance culture, and program design. These engagements can include program assessments, interviews, cultural audits, climate surveys, and other evaluative tools, and they increasingly intersect with complex regulatory environments and emerging technologies that further complicate compliance oversight. As boards navigate these requirements, they face consequential choices about when to engage outside consultants and which types of consultants to retain—choices that are often treated as routine but in fact carry significant governance implications.

This Article argues that boards must take seriously their responsibility to secure appropriate education for compliance oversight — a duty that often requires not just retaining outside consultants, but deliberately structuring, constraining, and governing those engagements so that the education boards receive is candid, independent, and aligned with the firm’s purpose and fiduciary commitments. The Article examines how differences in consultants’ constraints, incentives, and institutional positions may affect the education boards receive. Professional norms may help channel consultant behavior, but they are neither universal nor sufficient. Where consultants lack formal professional obligations, boards may bear greater responsibility for structuring engagements around clearly articulated, measurable standards rooted in the firm’s purpose, ethical commitments, and risk profile, and for defining expectations of candor, independence, and escalation. Ultimately, the question is not whether boards should engage compliance consultants to assist them—that is largely a foregone conclusion—but how boards can structure those engagements to ensure they are meaningfully educated for the oversight role they retain.

detail.abstract: The global economic order is undergoing a fundamental transformation as power shifts from a unipolar Western-dominated system toward a multipolar configuration. This research paper examines the emergence of economic multipolarity through three interconnected phenomena: the expansion of BRICS and formation of alternative economic blocs, de-dollarization trends in international finance, and the restructuring of global supply chains. With particular emphasis on India's strategic positioning, this study analyzes how the world's fifth-largest economy navigates this transition through its policy of strategic autonomy and multi-alignment. Drawing on recent data from 2024-2025, including BRICS expansion to ten members representing 37.3% of global GDP and the decline of dollar reserves to 57.3%, this paper employs mixedmethods analysis combining quantitative economic indicators with qualitative policy assessment. The findings reveal that while multipolarity creates opportunities for emerging economies to assert greater influence in global governance, it also introduces complexities including geopolitical tensions, coordination challenges, and the risk of fragmentation. For India, this transition presents a unique opportunity to position itself as a bridge between competing power centers while advancing its economic interests. The research contributes to understanding how middle powers can leverage multipolar dynamics to enhance their global standing without compromising sovereignty. This study concludes that economic multipolarity is not merely a redistribution of power but a fundamental reimagining of how nations collaborate, compete, and coexist in an interconnected world economy.

detail.abstract: We develop a comprehensive framework for modeling multivariate asset return distributions using characteristic functions (CFs). The CF approach offers fundamental advantages over density-based methods: it always exists, uniquely determines the distribution via the Lévy inversion theorem, and admits tractable closed forms for important non-Gaussian models including stable and tempered stable processes. We present eight parametric models-Gaussian, elliptical Student-t, Gaussian mixture, directional stable subordinator, tempered directional stable, low-rank Lévy copula jump factor, Gaussian-Schoenberg composite, and random frequency mixture-with complete mathematical derivations of their characteristic functions. We introduce a meta-t extension formulated directly in characteristic-function space, decoupling marginal behavior from Student-t tail dependence while preserving exact portfolio aggregation. On the statistical side, we develop a weighted L 2 distance metric for model comparison and a factorization defect test for detecting crosssectional dependence, complemented by distance correlation analysis. Empirical analysis of 16 US equities over 2014-2025 demonstrates that the Gaussian mixture model achieves the best fit, while all models exhibit significant cross-block dependence between technology and non-technology sectors. The portfolio projection identity ϕ w ⊤ X (t) = ϕ X (tw) is validated numerically at machine precision. Finally, we establish that law-invariant portfolio optimization problems can be formulated as functional optimization over one-dimensional CF restrictions, with classical meanvariance theory emerging as a second-order truncation of the log-characteristic function.
