Also aims to reflect the roots of noise pollution and the benefits of integrated tree plantation and increased forestry in reducing the noise pollution level. Thus, the various parts and areas of Dhaka city are noted for the projected work. Long-term research has been conducted on the harmful effects of noise pollution on both physical and mental health of human and the surrounding environment. Numerous studies have connected various health effects to both short-term and long-term noise exposure to living beings and the health. title: The Labour Market In The Euro Area: And Yet, It Moves!
affiliations: European Central Bank, ECB, European Central Bank (ECB) and

detail.title: The Labour Market In The Euro Area: And Yet, It Moves!
detail.abstract: Unlike past high-inflation episodes, the euro area labour market remained surprisingly resilient during the inflation surge of the early 2020s. This paper investigates the drivers of this resilience by combining long-span euro area macroeconomic data (1970–2025) with a structural VAR analysis that disentangles the roles of aggregate demand and supply, monetary policy, and factor-substitution shocks. Our findings show that, in contrast to the 1970s and 1980s, the decline in real wages has supported labour demand and, more broadly, the labour market, thereby helping to explain the decoupling between output and employment. We also find that monetary policy shocks have had a stronger impact on output than on employment,further amplifying the pro-cyclicality of labour productivity.

title:
Interest Rates, Monetary Credibility, and Currency Stabilization
A Review of a Gradual Disinflation Strategy for Iran with Lessons from Türkiye and Cambodia
affiliations: King Mongkut’s Institute of Technology Ladkrabang

detail.title:
Interest Rates, Monetary Credibility, and Currency Stabilization
A Review of a Gradual Disinflation Strategy for Iran with Lessons from Türkiye and Cambodia
detail.abstract: Iran's repeated inflation episodes and the long-term depreciation of the rial are commonly linked to external constraints, including sanctions and reduced access to hard currency. Nevertheless, international evidence from high-inflation economies shows that domestic monetary governance, banking-sector behavior, fiscal dominance, and credibility failures can be equally important. This review assesses a pragmatic stabilization proposal that focuses on a three-year, preannounced interest-rate reduction path (for instance, 30% → 20% → 10% → ~1%), combined with a shift away from exclusive dollar dependence through greater use of the Chinese yuan and, potentially, a managed dual-currency setting (rial and yuan) for certain transactions. Using Türkiye's post-2021 experience where unconventional rate cuts coincided with a sharp inflation surge and Cambodia's long-run experience with extensive foreigncurrency use as comparative reference points, the article evaluates the feasibility, mechanisms, risks, and institutional requirements of the proposed policy package. The central conclusion is that interest-rate reductions can contribute to stabilization only when embedded in a credible macroeconomic framework: banking-sector repair, limitations on monetary financing, transparent fiscal discipline, and clear communication to re-anchor expectations. Without these complements, aggressive rate cuts risk worsening inflation and accelerating currency substitution.

title: Money Demand By Non-Financial Corporations
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Money Demand By Non-Financial Corporations
detail.abstract: We document empirically the money demand by European non-financial corporations by exploiting a unique and brand-new survey on their cash usage in a stress period. We also assess: (i) the relation between cash held and firm size; and (ii) estimate point values of cash holdings and carry out statistical comparisons along the sectoral and country dimensions. First, we find that cash holdings are inversely related to firm size, providing additional evidence that Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) tend to store more cash relative to their larger peers. Second, we find that cash-intensive sectors and” cash-friendly” countries display right-shifted distributions of cash holdings with statistically-significant larger average holdings. We argue that in a low interest rate and low inflation environment cash holdings serve as a store of value for European firms, in particular for SMEs which are more likely to be financially constrained, especially in crisis times.

title: Subjective Well-being and Public Policy

detail.title: Subjective Well-being and Public Policy
detail.abstract: (This paper gives an overview of the idea of subjective well-being which has captured the attention of the economists in the last one decade or so. The gist of the literature which has emerged on the subject is that income or GDP does not truly reflect human welfare and there is need to make use of interdisciplinary knowledge to develop a new metrics to measure it. Plausible explanations of income-happiness paradox are presented besides shedding light on the shortcomings of GDP as yardstick of development. The determinants and building blocks of happiness, both at individual and societal level, are discussed and public policy prescriptions, in the light of lessons drawn from the World Happiness Reports, are prescribed for enhancing subjective well-being of the people with particular reference to Pakistan).

title: Analyzing Pakistan's National Competitiveness

detail.title: Analyzing Pakistan's National Competitiveness
detail.abstract: (The idea of national competitiveness has gained prominence in the last two decades or so. National competitiveness, as originally understood by the economists, only meant exchange rate engineering to enhance exports. The concept has evolved and expanded in scope with the passage of time. However, consensus does not exist with regard to its definition and determinants. Three international reports i.e. Global Competitiveness Report of WEF, the World Competitiveness Year Book of IMD, and Doing Business of the World Bank are now well recognized reports which rank countries on the ladder of international competitiveness every year. These reports may not be perfect assessments of countries’ competitiveness. But, they, however, give a fair idea of their standing on the ladder of international competitiveness. Out of these reports, the Global Competitiveness Report of WEF and Doing Business of the World Bank evaluate Pakistan’s national competitiveness every year. An analysis of Pakistan’s rankings determined by these reports indicates that Pakistan remains stuck up in low equilibrium of national competitiveness. The main reasons underlying low national competitiveness of Pakistan include political instability, inadequately educated workforce, corruption, hurdles in access to finance, poor linkages between the academia and industry, crumbling infrastructure, regulatory and administrative bottlenecks, and low social development. Based on analysis through the lens of these international reports, the paper concludes that Pakistan needs to reprioritize public spending by making more investment in social sector particularly education, healthcare, and skill development. Author)

title: Fiscal Seigniorage And Price Level Determination In A Currency Union
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Fiscal Seigniorage And Price Level Determination In A Currency Union

keywords: fiscal theory of the price level

detail.abstract: I study price level determination in a currency union when some member countries’ government securities earn a convenience yield. These ”convenience assets” generate fiscal seigniorage revenues that, given appropriate fiscal and monetary policies, back the union’s price level, much like primary surpluses and monetary seigniorage do. An exogenous drop in the private-sector demand for convenience assets reduces seigniorage revenues and raises the price level. It also results in a wealth transfer across countries owing to the heterogeneity in convenience yields.

title: Beyond Rashi: Rashbam's Groundbreaking Peshat Approach and the Battle Over Biblical Truth
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY) - Koppelman School of Business

detail.title: Beyond Rashi: Rashbam's Groundbreaking Peshat Approach and the Battle Over Biblical Truth
detail.abstract: Rabbi Shmuel ben Meir (Rashbam), grandson of the legendary Rashi, produced one of medieval Judaism's most innovative and controversial biblical commentaries. While his grandfather sought to balance text and tradition, Rashbam insisted on interpreting Scripture according to its plain meaning (peshat) alone. He often openly rejected explanations from the Talmud and Midrash when they conflicted with the literal text, an audacious approach that led to centuries of suppression. His commentary on Genesis disappeared for hundreds of years, and even today, certain Orthodox publishers continue to censor his work. This study examines Rashbam's distinctive methodology, specifically his revolutionary distinction between peshat and halacha. By analyzing his most provocative interpretations, including the claim that biblical days of creation began in the morning, that wearing tefillin is rabbinical, and the assertion that Joseph's brothers never actually sold him, this paper demonstrates why Rashbam remains both essential to traditional scholarship. Ultimately, this article argues that the distinction between peshat and derash is crucial for avoiding educational miseducation. Rashbam's work serves as a powerful reminder that intellectual honesty and faithfulness to the text need not conflict with religious commitment.

title: Climate Change, Catastrophes, Insurance And The Macroeconomy
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB), European Central Bank (ECB), Bank of England, European Central Bank (ECB), , , European Central Bank (ECB) and

detail.title: Climate Change, Catastrophes, Insurance And The Macroeconomy
detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of insurance in mitigating the adverse macroeconomic effects of climate-related catastrophes. We first develop a stylised theoretical growth model which incorporates a role for natural catastrophes, climate change and insurance. This illustrates how insurance can mitigate the impact of catastrophes and articulates the potential effect of falling insurance coverage as global warming intensifies. The model also provides a basis for our empirical analysis which explores the link between insurance coverage and the macroeconomic impact of catastrophes for a sample of several thousand disaster events across 47 developed and middle income countries between 1996 and 2019. The results confirm that higher insurance coverage is associated with less severe macroeconomic consequences of disasters. With climate-related catastrophes becoming ever more frequent and severe, our findings highlight the importance of developing policies to reduce the climate insurance protection gap.

title: Nowcasting Economic Growth with Machine Learning and Satellite Data
affiliations: , International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and University College Dublin

detail.title: Nowcasting Economic Growth with Machine Learning and Satellite Data

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The absence of reliable data on fundamental economic indicators (e.g. real GDP), combined with structural shifts in the economy, can severely constrain the ability to conduct accurate macroeconomic analysis and forecasting. This paper explores alternatives to address data limitations by integrating machine learning and satellite data to estimate real GDP. Specifically, it finds that incorporating satellite-based nightlight data into a random forest model significantly improves the accuracy of quarterly GDP growth estimates compared with models relying solely on traditional indicators. This empirical application contributes to the emerging nowcasting field to enhance economic forecasting in economies with significant data gaps.

title: Church and State Cooperation: Bishop Opposition in the First Vatican
affiliations: Texas Tech University - Free Market Institute

detail.title: Church and State Cooperation: Bishop Opposition in the First Vatican
detail.abstract: I apply the tools of economic analysis to explain a bishop's opposition to the decrees of the First Vatican Council (ca. 1869-1970). The First Vatican Council limited the extent bishops could cooperate with non-Catholic governments. I use historical data to explain the relationships between countries and the Catholic Church to give background about the extent of secular influence the Church possessed in the 19th century. Additionally, I use a model of church and state cooperation to explain the differences in how bishops voted during the council. I find that bishops who come from countries with governments that legitimize themselves by employing a mixed bundle of Catholic and non-Catholic ideological sources were more likely to oppose the definition of decrees of the Council.

title: Toward a Fixed-Point Formulation of American Option Pricing
affiliations: University of Bari

detail.title: Toward a Fixed-Point Formulation of American Option Pricing
detail.abstract: We present a fixed point approach to American option pricing that unifies optimal stopping theory, variational inequalities, and numerical methods. By properly formulating the problem as a global fixed point equation on a product Banach space and establishing both metric (contraction) and order-theoretic (monotone operator) properties, we provide comprehensive theoretical justification for computational schemes. Our framework explicitly connects the Snell envelope characterization with both Banach contraction theory (under a strict contraction condition for the global operator) and an order-theoretic monotone operator viewpoint (valid for all r ≥ 0), resolving ambiguities in previous formulations. We introduce policy iteration as the natural algorithmic manifestation of the fixed point perspective, establishing clear connections to linear complementarity problems and practical computational methods.

title: Public-Private Partnerships in the Development of Smart Cities in the Gulf States: Models, Economic Benefits, and Challenges
affiliations: Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO)

detail.title: Public-Private Partnerships in the Development of Smart Cities in the Gulf States: Models, Economic Benefits, and Challenges
detail.abstract: In the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, the development of smart cities has become a key element of national strategies for economic diversification and digitalization. For the successful implementation of these strategies, public-private partnerships (PPPs) serve as an effective mechanism for mobilizing private investment and expertise while simultaneously reducing fiscal burdens and ensuring balanced risksharing. This paper examines the institutional foundations of PPPs in the region, models of implementation, and completed projects within the smart-city agenda. Using Masdar City and NEOM as case studies, the text highlights a distinctive feature of such PPP projects: their multisectoral nature, simultaneously covering ICT, energy, transport, and housing construction. The analysis identifies key benefits, including investment inflows, accelerated project delivery, improved service quality, and the deployment of advanced technologies. At the same time, it highlights challenges such as contractual complexity, significant transaction costs, shortages of qualified personnel, and the need for transparency. The paper concludes that PPPs in the Gulf are an optimal model for smartcity delivery, aligning public priorities with private resources and innovation.

title: Transfer Pricing Regulations and Dispute Resolution Mechanisms: A Critical Legal Analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Transfer Pricing Regulations and Dispute Resolution Mechanisms: A Critical Legal Analysis
detail.abstract: Transfer pricing is nowadays one of the most challenging and debatable fields of international taxation due to the growing globalization of multinational enterprises (MNEs) as well as intra-group transactions across the borders. Governments of countries around the globe have intensified the transfer pricing rules to prevent base erosion and profit shifting resulting in an increase in the transfer prices controversies. Such conflicts have a tendency of creating a situation of double taxation, long litigation and ambiguity among taxpayers. International organizations, especially the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) have in turn, advocated dispute resolution methods including Mutual Agreement Procedures (MAP), Advance Pricing Agreements (APAs), arbitration and domestic dispute resolution systems. The critical legal analysis of transfer pricing regulations and dispute resolution mechanisms of this research paper will be conducted using only the materials of OECD, academic literature, IBFD research, and professional legal analyses. The paper discusses the effectiveness, constraints and realistic issues of the current dispute resolution systems and specifically the MAP under BEPS Action 14, APAs and regional systems like the European Union dispute resolution system. It postulates that although much has been done to enhance the process of dispute resolution, there are structural weaknesses, delays, capacity and asymmetry in power between tax authorities and taxpayers that still brings down its efficacy. This paper ends by making recommendations on how to make the transparency, consistency, and taxpayer confidence on the system of the transfer pricing dispute resolution.

title: Interest Rates and Inflation Dynamics: Short-Run Cost-Channel Evidence from a Multi-Country Panel Study (2019-2023)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Interest Rates and Inflation Dynamics: Short-Run Cost-Channel Evidence from a Multi-Country Panel Study (2019-2023)
detail.abstract: This paper provides a rigorous empirical investigation of the short-run relationship between nominal interest rates and inflation, focusing on the cost-channel of monetary transmission. Utilizing an unbalanced panel dataset of 40 developed and developing economies from 2019 to 2023-a period characterized by significant supply shocks and shifting monetary policy stances-the study employs both Fixed Effects (FE) and System Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimators to address endogeneity concerns. The core finding is a statistically significant positive relationship: a one-percentage-point increase in the nominal lending rate is associated with an approximate 0.3 percentage point increase in Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation. This effect is markedly stronger in developing economies, indicating a more potent cost-channel where higher financing costs are rapidly transmitted to consumer prices. The results challenge the conventional view of an unconditionally inverse short-run policy relationship, highlighting the potential for monetary tightening to exert inflationary pressure through production-cost channels under specific conditions. The study concludes with nuanced implications for monetary policy, emphasizing the need for calibrated approaches, especially in credit-dependent emerging markets.

title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Occupational Structure and the Gender Wage Gap
affiliations: University of Graz, University of Graz, University of Graz and Copenhagen Business School

detail.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Occupational Structure and the Gender Wage Gap
detail.abstract: We provide new evidence on how wage differences across firms shape the gender wage gap and highlight the role of gendered occupational segregation. We show that when occupations are omitted from canonical AKM models, the estimated firm effects mechanically absorb occupation-specific wage differences. We illustrate this mechanism through simulations and then quantify its empirical relevance using Danish register data. The estimated contribution of firm sorting to the gender wage gap declines by up to 30% once occupations are accounted for. Furthermore, around 90% of firm sorting occurs between industries, with women disproportionately employed in lower-paying ones. Our results demonstrate that gendered firm sorting is closely intertwined with occupational and industry segregation.

title: Poverty as a Discursive Infrastructure: Framing Effects, Economic Agency, and Urban Marginalization in the Philippines
affiliations: and Google Inc.

detail.title: Poverty as a Discursive Infrastructure: Framing Effects, Economic Agency, and Urban Marginalization in the Philippines
detail.abstract: This qualitative research investigates the constitutive role of communicative framing in the production and internalization of economic poverty among urban poor residents in Manila, Philippines. Anchored in the framing theory and situated within a communication-centric analytic paradigm, the study utilizes semi-structured interviews to examine how macro-level discursive formations emanating from state, media, and institutional actors are translated into micro-level interpretive schemas through which marginalized subjects perceive economic deprivation, agency, and futurity. The analysis demonstrates that participants' narratives are permeated by hegemonic frames of dependency, passivity, and moralized deservingness, which operate as symbolic constraints that delimit perceived economic agency and normalize structural exclusion. The study contends that communication functions not merely as a descriptive or mediating apparatus but as an infrastructural dimension of economic inequality itself, actively configuring the conditions of possibility for economic action. To deepen the paper's theoretical portability, we introduce the Communicative Architecture of Governed Exclusion (CAGE) as a mid-range framework specifying how poverty is reproduced through 1) classification (what counts as poverty and who counts as poor); 2) access control (administrative and informational gatekeeping); 3) governance through discourse (moralized narratives of deservingness and dependency); and 4) exclusion effects (internalized passivity, "waiting orientation," and selflimiting economic agency). CAGE clarifies how framing effects become durable social infrastructure-an architecture that governs inclusion and exclusion through everyday communication.

title: The Output Convergence Debate Revisited: Lessons from Recent Developments in the Analysis of Panel Data Models
affiliations: University of Cambridge and Birkbeck, University of London

detail.title: The Output Convergence Debate Revisited: Lessons from Recent Developments in the Analysis of Panel Data Models
detail.abstract: This paper provides a critical examination of the empirical basis of the output convergence debate in the light of recent developments in the analysis of dynamic heterogeneous panels with interactive effects. It shows that popular tools such as Barro's cross-country regressions and two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimators that assume parallel trends and homogeneous dynamics lead to substantial under-estimation of the speed of convergence and misleading inference. Instead, dynamic common correlated effects (DCCE) estimators due to Chudik and Pesaran (2015a) provide consistent estimates and valid inference that are robust to nonparallel trends and correlated heterogeneity and apply even if there are breaks, trends and/or unit roots in the latent technology factor. It also suggests a way to estimate the effect of slowly moving determinants of growth. The theoretical findings are augmented with empirical evidence using Penn World Tables data, finding little evidence of per capita output convergence across countries, very slow evidence of cross country growth convergence, and reasonably fast within country convergence. Capital accumulation is found to be the most important single determinant of cross-country differences in output while slow moving indicators such as potential for conflict and protection of property rights proved to be statistically significant determinants of the steady state levels of output per capita. We are also able to replicate a positive evidence of democratization on output, but we find that the statistical significance of this effect to fall as we allow for nonparallel trends and dynamic heterogeneity.

title: Do Research Universities Recession-Proof Their Regions? Evidence from State Flagship College Towns
affiliations: University of Greenwich and

detail.title: Do Research Universities Recession-Proof Their Regions? Evidence from State Flagship College Towns

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Philadelphia Working Paper No. 26-8
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Using synthetic differences-in-differences models, we study whether U.S. counties containing state flagship universities experienced resiliency via lower unemployment rates during the past three U.S. recessions. We find an insignificant effect for the 2001 recession and a large resiliency effect for the 2008-2009 recession. However, counties with flagship universities faced higher unemployment rates during the 2020 recession, and were therefore less resilient to the Covid-19 recession than other counties. These results support the hypothesis that stable consumption demand for non-tradables drives resiliency, which was absent during the 2020 recession when most university campuses were closed to students due to Covid-19 restrictions.

title: Deadweight Drift: A Unified Framework for Market Distortions
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Deadweight Drift: A Unified Framework for Market Distortions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently with no personal or financial relationships that could have influenced the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical/conceptual paper involving no human participants, patient data, or case studies.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. Self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes Deadweight Drift as a generalization of Deadweight Loss that unifies institutional and behavioral market distortions under a single theoretical concept. Vernon Smith's experimental economics demonstrated that equilibrium models succeed remarkably well in nonspeculative markets but systematically fail in speculative markets; findings that remain theoretically disconnected in the literature. This paper argues that a structural feature explains this divergence: in ordinary markets, goods are purchased for consumption, anchoring prices to use value; in speculative markets, assets are purchased for resale, decoupling prices from fundamental value and enabling behavioral dynamics to generate sustained deviations from equilibrium. Deadweight Drift bridges this gap by defining market distortion as cumulative deviation from equilibrium regardless of source, operating in two directions: Negative Drift (activity suppressed below equilibrium) and Positive Drift (activity inflated above equilibrium). The framework achieves theoretical unification through subtraction rather than addition: traditional Deadweight Loss becomes a special case of externally-induced Negative Drift, while speculative bubbles and panics become internally-induced Positive and Negative Drift respectively. The economic consequence, capital not allocated to its most productive use, is identical across all cases. This parsimonious framework extends explanatory power to speculative markets while maintaining the analytical clarity of the original Deadweight Loss concept.

title: New Atheism and Islam: (A Critical Examination of Scientism, Morality, and Islamic Intellectual Responses in the Post-2000 Era)
affiliations: Superior University

detail.title: New Atheism and Islam: (A Critical Examination of Scientism, Morality, and Islamic Intellectual Responses in the Post-2000 Era)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This manuscript offers an analytical examination of New Atheism’s engagement with Islam, focusing on epistemological assumptions, moral reasoning, and interpretive frameworks rather than polemical or apologetic argumentation. The study aims to contribute to contemporary debates in religious studies and philosophy of religion by distinguishing science from scientism and by situating Islamic intellectual responses within both classical and modern contexts. I confirm that this submission is original, has not been published elsewhere, and is not under consideration by another journal. I would be grateful for the editor’s assessment regarding its suitability for the journal’s scope.

detail.abstract: New Atheism, which emerged in the early 2000s, represents a clear shift from earlier forms of atheism. Unlike classical atheism, which mainly focused on philosophical questions about whether God exists, New Atheism functions more as a cultural and mediadriven movement. It openly criticizes religion especially Islam by portraying it as irrational, morally backward, and opposed to science.

title: AI, Information Depth, and the Collapse of Shallow Signal Predictability Evidence from a 40-Year Structural Break in Equity Markets
affiliations: University of Liège - HEC-Liège, Management School of the University of Liège

detail.title: AI, Information Depth, and the Collapse of Shallow Signal Predictability Evidence from a 40-Year Structural Break in Equity Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available secondary data and does not involve human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: We investigate whether AI democratization has altered the relative effectiveness of quantitative sentiment-based trading versus patient fundamental analysis in high-tech equity markets. Analyzing 40 years of data (1985-2025) across 200 firms and 154,796 news articles, we document a dramatic reversal: Democratized Quantitative Sentiment Strategies (DQSS) mimicking accessible algorithmic approaches collapsed from +75.4% cumulative returns (2012-2019) to-92.3% (2022-2025), while Buffett-Style fundamental Portfolios (BSP) surged from +68.2% to +84.6%-a 176.9 percentage point reversal (t=8.47***). This shift reflects asymmetric AI effects: information extraction costs for shallow sentiment data approached zero (predictive power declined 60.9%), while costs for deep fundamental analysis remained high (patent quality predictive power increased 35.5%). We introduce replicability asymmetry as an organizing principle: AI democratization destroys advantages for accessible quantitative strategies while leaving temperament-based advantages intact. Our findings validate adaptive markets hypothesis with a clear technological catalyst and provide actionable guidance for asset managers controlling $50+ trillion globally.

title: A Note on Extremism (with Special Reference to Norm Entrepreneurs and Habituation)
affiliations: Harvard Law School

detail.title: A Note on Extremism (with Special Reference to Norm Entrepreneurs and Habituation)
detail.abstract: Extremism is often made possible or fueled by group polarization: Like-minded people, engaged in discussions with one another, adopt a more extreme position in line with their prediscussion inclinations. Group polarization often promotes and influences norm entrepreneurs, who in turn help direct, unify, and energize those who listen to them, who in turn direct and energize norm enterpreneurs. The result can be a kind of spiral or tornado. Because of habituation, understood as diminishing sensitivity to stimuli, the energy provided by a transgressive or outre position is often less intense on Wednesday than it was on Monday, which means that norm entrepreneurs are often incentivized to up the ante. Spare as they are, these points suggest the importance of seeing extremism as a product of dynamic interactions among (1) group polarization; (2) norm entrepreneurship; and (3) habituation and thrill-seeking. These interactions might be formalized and subjected to empirical testing.

title: Earnings Information Spillovers and Depositor Contagion
affiliations: Duke University - Fuqua School of Business, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School - Finance Department , Duke University and

detail.title: Earnings Information Spillovers and Depositor Contagion
detail.abstract: Understanding the nature of interconnections between banks is crucial to the knowledge of financial contagions and the appropriate policy response. We examine interconnections in the U.S. banking industry that stem from earnings information spillovers from local peers. Using a sample of nearly 8,800 commercial banks over three decades, we find that uninsured deposit flows respond strongly to the performance of peer banks – particularly when peers perform poorly but not when they perform well. Exploring the mechanisms, we find that the earnings information spillovers operate through both asset commonalities and panic-driven behaviors wherein depositors withdraw out of concerns about early withdrawals by other depositors. Our findings inform theories of contagion and their policy implications.

title: Creativity as Data and the Copyright-Privacy Interface
affiliations: UCLA School of Law - UCLA School of Law

detail.title: Creativity as Data and the Copyright-Privacy Interface

publicationDetails.detailsText: UCLA School of Law, Public Law Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: University of California, Los Angeles School of Law, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Copyright is having its data privacy moment. Many pillars of the growing AI infrastructure—the training of large language models, newer retrieval augmented generation (RAG) processes, and the future of agentic AI workflows—require access to millions of copyrighted works, mining creative works not for their expressive purpose but for their data value. Copyright law, with its focus on protecting creative expression and on individualized, ex-post infringement proceedings, is currently unequipped to answer large scale questions about whether such datafication is legally permissible.

We have been here once before. In the field of privacy law, long standing notions of what privacy was—as dignitarian rights focused on individualized transgressions—were similarly disrupted with the arrival of mass surveillance tools and data mining, which extracted value not from one-off transactions, but instead from information processed at scale. This Article argues that copyright, too, is now at a similar crossroads, and that it might learn from the parallel, more heavily theorized field of privacy law in answering the question of whether copyright could, or should, accommodate the datafication of creative works. 

In making the analogy to privacy law, this Article draws out several key insights. The first is the theoretical insight that AI's mass reproduction of copyrighted works is not simply different in degree from past technological developments, but fundamentally different in kind, extracting value by drawing out large-scale patterns among many (many) copyrighted works. The second is the doctrinal insight that judges need not adhere to formalistic applications of some static conception of the law; as privacy scholars have documented, cases that confronted technological changes differing in kind from those that came before might sometimes call for parallel revolutions in the law. Finally, looking to privacy law draws out the prescriptive insight that copyright's individualized, case-by-case dispute resolution model, focused on highly fact-specific doctrines like fair use, is increasingly outdated in a world of mass infringement. The age of mass reproduction requires an ex-ante regulatory, not a transactional, copyright.

detail.abstract:
The UK Intellectual Property Office (IPO) has been tracking consumer behaviour (among the 12+ population in the UK) in relation to online copyright infringement since 2012. Now in its 13th wave of survey data, the Online Copyright Infringement (OCI) tracker has established itself as a comprehensive and insightful study in this space. Globally, Australia, Canada and Germany have sought to replicate the study and the IPO is hopeful that other countries will follow.

The study itself focuses on specific content categories, looking at infringement behaviours as well as other topics that help to contextualise and explain them. Given the rapid nature of technological advancements, the study is currently conducted biannually to ensure that the IPO can monitor the influence of new online platforms on infringement behaviours.

Findings from the IPO’s OCI studies are widely shared and help to inform high-level decision-making. This includes monitoring infringement behaviours, tracking the effectiveness of educational campaigns looking to mitigate such behaviours, facilitating evidence-based policy making and liaising with stakeholders within the relevant content industries.

title: Lessons on State and Local Income Taxes from the Twenty-first Century and Challenges for the Future
affiliations: University of California, Irvine

detail.title: Lessons on State and Local Income Taxes from the Twenty-first Century and Challenges for the Future
detail.abstract: I survey the research on the last twenty-five years of subnational income tax policy and conclude that the defining feature of state and local income taxes is geography. Geographic boundaries limit the power of subnational governments to tax people and activities. The article discusses where income should be taxed and the behavioral effects of these tax rules on the interjurisdictional mobility of people and jobs. I then examine how this mobility can heighten tax competition, which in turn can limit the ability of state and local governments to engage in progressive redistribution. I include a discussion of how telework will influence the future of the income tax by decoupling the locations of the employee and employer. Important areas for future research for the coming decades are highlighted throughout the article.

title: Inflation and Human Capital Investment Decisions
affiliations: and

detail.title: Inflation and Human Capital Investment Decisions
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of inflation on human capital investment decisions. Using a specially designed survey we estimate the causal effect of recent price level increases on the graduation plans of over 1,200 U.S. university students. We find that inflation caused over half of the respondents to alter their plans, with nearly 60 percent of these opting to accumulate less human capital and the remainder increasing their human capital by taking additional courses or pursuing double majors or advanced degrees. A comparison of empirical treatment estimates to predictions derived from our theoretical framework reveals that inflation-driven higher direct costs reduced human capital investments, particularly among those for whom inflation had reduced their ability to pay bills. Conversely, while some students merely postponed graduation because they believed inflation would not persist, higher inflation-induced uncertainty in the post-graduation labor market generally caused greater human capital accumulation, especially among economically vulnerable students and those whose confidence in finding a job after graduation had declined. The study concludes with policy implications, contributing new insights into how macroeconomic shocks affect educational choices.

title: Demand for Home Pension and Reverse Mortgage: An Information Provision Survey Experiment
affiliations: Yonsei University and Bank of Korea - Economic Research Institute

detail.title: Demand for Home Pension and Reverse Mortgage: An Information Provision Survey Experiment
detail.abstract: Population aging and the sustainability of retirement financing are critical challenges facing many developed economies. In South Korea, elderly poverty remains a critical issue, despite widespread homeownership among older adults. Although the home pension program allows retirees to unlock housing wealth, uptake remains below 2% as of 2024. Using a large-scale survey of adults aged 55–79, we conduct an information provision experiment to assess how policy reforms and belief corrections affect demand. We find that enrollment intention rises by 6 percentage points when monthly pension payments are adjusted with house price changes, and by 5 percentage points when bequest conditions are made more flexible. Notably, merely informing that the fixed monthly payments—often perceived as disadvantageous during housing price increases—do not result in a loss when house prices rise because the amount bequeathed to their children increases accordingly, led to a 7%p increase in enrollment intention. Our results suggest that addressing informational barriers may be as effective as structural reforms in increasing program uptake.

title: Guns and Butter: The Fiscal Consequences of Rearmament and War
affiliations: and Kiel Institute for the World Economy

detail.title: Guns and Butter: The Fiscal Consequences of Rearmament and War
detail.abstract: We study the fiscal consequences of large military buildups. To do so, we assemble the Global Budget Database, a comprehensive dataset of disaggregated central government finances for 20 countries from 1870 to 2022. We identify 114 episodes of military spending booms, in peace and war, and analyze their financing and long-term fiscal legacy. Consistent with theory, wartime booms are financed primarily through debt, while peacetime booms rely on a more balanced mix of debt and taxes. In contrast to the classic notion of “guns versus butter,” we find little evidence that social spending is cut during military expansions. Instead, when societies rearm, they tend to choose guns and butter, resulting in higher debt, expenditures, and taxes. Debt rises and later falls, but tax rates and tax revenues remain elevated for 15 years or more. Large geopolitical shocks, in war and peace, result in higher taxes and a lasting fiscal expansion.

title: The Potential and Utility of Land Value Taxation: A Theoretical Framework and Simulation for China
affiliations: Syracuse University, CEPR and Central University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: The Potential and Utility of Land Value Taxation: A Theoretical Framework and Simulation for China
detail.abstract: This paper develops an analytical framework for examining land taxation in the context of contemporary urban economies. We dissect the China case for simulation, comparing two model-based scenarios where revenue losses from consumption taxes are replaced by higher income taxes and land taxes. We calibrate the model to year-2015 data and find that higher income taxes cause large losses in output and income, while higher land taxes lead to substantive gains that increase with land share in net wealth. This paper offers empirical explorations in revitalizing the land tax, with simulation results at a large country level for generalization.

title: An Unholy Alliance: The Relationship Between Organized Crime and Corruption in Italy
affiliations: and Illinois State University - Department of Economics

detail.title: An Unholy Alliance: The Relationship Between Organized Crime and Corruption in Italy
detail.abstract: We investigate the long-run relationship between organized crime and corruption using data from 20 Italian regions over 30 years. As Rose-Ackerman and Palifka (2018) argue, corruption and organized crime often go together. Our study contributes to the literature in several ways in terms of empirical methodology and specification. We account for integration and cointegration properties of the data and estimate the cointegrating relationship between organized crime and corruption using Fully Modified Ordinary Least Squares (FMOLS), following Pedroni (2000). Our findings are twofold. First, according to our FMOLS estimates, organized crime increases corruption, and this effect becomes stronger as government spending increases. Second, there is bidirectional Granger causality between corruption and organized crime. Our results are robust to alternative specifications and different estimation methods. Overall, our findings point to a persistent and mutually reinforcing relationship between organized crime and corruption, which has significant consequences for implementing anti-corruption policies.

title: Expected Insurance Coverage and Pharmaceutical Innovation: Evidence from China's National Drug Price Negotiation Policy
affiliations: Tsinghua University - School of Economics & Management, PBCSF, Tsinghua University,  and

detail.title: Expected Insurance Coverage and Pharmaceutical Innovation: Evidence from China's National Drug Price Negotiation Policy
detail.abstract: How can developing countries foster pharmaceutical innovation when drug price negotiations risk eroding firms' incentives? China's National Drug Price Negotiation policy addresses this challenge by pairing substantial price cuts with expanded insurance coverage for innovative drugs, enlarging the effective market size. We examine its impact on innovation using a difference-in-differences design that compares clinical trials of new drugs (treated) with those of vaccines (untreated) in each disease group. The policy increases the number of trials by 0.56 per disease per year. The effects are particularly pronounced for more novel innovations and similar for domestic and foreign firms. We also find that the policy induces more pharmaceutical R&D firms, especially those of small size, to enter the market. Finally, we document increased collaboration and outsourcing across firms.

title: Oral Cancer Detection in Orthodontic Practice: A Clinical Review

detail.title: Oral Cancer Detection in Orthodontic Practice: A Clinical Review

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract: Background: Orthodontists are uniquely positioned within dental practice to detect early-stage oral malignancies and potentially malignant disorders. Their role includes repeated, longitudinal examination of the oral mucosa in patients across all age groups, offering sustained opportunities for opportunistic screening. This review synthesises current evidence on oral cancer recognition, risk stratification, and referral pathways relevant to orthodontic practice. Methods: This is a narrative review informed by Cochrane systematic reviews on diagnostic test accuracy, screening, and clinical assessment of oral cancer and potentially malignant disorders. Additional sources include global cancer registry data (GLOBOCAN), international consensus guidelines, and standard oral pathology references. Results: Oral cancer frequently presents as persistent, non-healing ulcers or mixed red-white patches (erythroleukoplakia). Early-stage lesions are often asymptomatic and may be mistaken for traumatic irritation from orthodontic appliances. A 2021 Cochrane systematic review (63 studies, 7,942 lesions) concluded that insufficient accuracy exists for any adjunctive deviceincluding oral cytology, vital staining, or light-based detection-to replace histopathological examination of incisional biopsy. Oral cytology demonstrated the highest pooled accuracy (sensitivity 0.90; specificity 0.94) but cannot discriminate between dysplasia and invasive carcinoma. Conventional oral examination in asymptomatic populations exhibits highly variable sensitivity (0.50-0.99); a substantial proportion of early cancers are missed during routine visual inspection. Population-based visual screening reduces oral cancer mortality only in high-risk tobacco and alcohol users (RR 0.76). Emerging risk factors include cannabis smoking (possible association, confounded by tobacco), immunosuppression, and inherited bone marrow failure syndromes. Conclusions: Orthodontists contribute meaningfully to early diagnosis through systematic mucosal examination, recognition of high-risk clinical features, and established low-threshold referral pathways. Cochrane evidence confirms that incisional biopsy remains the diagnostic gold standard and that no in-office adjunctive technology is adequate for definitive diagnosis. Routine mucosal examination is standard clinical care, although population-wide screening programmes are not currently evidence-supported. A structured chairside checklist is proposed to operationalise opportunistic cancer detection in orthodontic practice. Novelty and Contribution: This review is the first to synthesise Cochrane diagnostic evidence specifically within an orthodontic clinical context and proposes a structured chairside detection checklist tailored to orthodontic practice. Disclaimer: This paper is a preprint and has not been certified by peer review. It reports early-stage research and should not be used to guide clinical practice or health-related behaviour without independent verification.

title: Data-Driven Journey Archetypes in Senior Care Decision-Making: A Behavioral Segmentation Model

detail.title: Data-Driven Journey Archetypes in Senior Care Decision-Making: A Behavioral Segmentation Model

keywords: Healthcare UX JEL Classification I18 -Health: Government Policy

detail.abstract: This paper presents an empirical framework for segmenting senior care decision-makers using behavioral signal data, moving beyond traditional demographics or static personas. Drawing from a structured dataset of 2,701 senior living inquiries, the study identifies five decision archetypes-each representing a unique combination of urgency, care intent, priorities, and confidence barriers. Through canonical field mapping and synthetic agent simulations, we demonstrate how journey paths, stall risks, and decision triggers can be modeled and predicted. The results indicate that early behavioral cues can reliably inform personalized engagement strategies, reduce friction, and enable predictive routing in digital CRM and care navigation systems.

title: Ramsey Alignment and the Postwar Tax System
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: Ramsey Alignment and the Postwar Tax System
detail.abstract: Was the postwar shift from corporate to personal taxation welfare-improving? I develop a sufficient statistics framework to evaluate the alignment of the tax system with the Ramsey optimum in dynamic general equilibrium. Alignment is captured by the angle between two vectors: one measuring each tax's first-order welfare cost, the other measuring its fiscal externality. Using narrative tax shocks, I estimate present-value tax elasticities that capture own-and cross-base spillovers in dynamic general equilibrium. These spillovers are quantitatively important: potential welfare gains from optimal reform were 0.7% of GDP in the 1950s, an order of magnitude larger than static partial equilibrium would suggest. By the 2020s, gains had fallen to 0.05% as reductions in effective corporate tax rates brought the system to near-optimality.

title: Time and Asset Aggregation in Stochastic Volatility Models: A Unified Theory of Distributional Convergence
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: Time and Asset Aggregation in Stochastic Volatility Models: A Unified Theory of Distributional Convergence
detail.abstract: We develop a unified theory of distributional convergence for portfolio returns under two complementary aggregation mechanisms: time aggregation (T → ∞), driven by ergodicity of the latent variance process, and asset aggregation (n → ∞), driven by cross-sectional central limit theorems in factor structures. The foundational insight is the variance-mixture representation: returns are conditionally Gaussian given integrated variance IV T = T 0 V t dt, so departures from Gaussianity are governed by fluctuations in IV T. Our main contributions are threefold. First, excess kurtosis decays as γ 2 (r T) = 3σ 2 /(κ 2 θT)+ o(T-1) under time aggregation, with explicit constant determined by the long-run covariance of integrated variance. This quantifies how volatility persistence (small κ) and vol-of-vol (large σ) slow convergence to Gaussianity. Second, idiosyncratic kurtosis decays as O(n-1) under diversification, while factor kurtosis persists at any fixed horizon-diversification eliminates idiosyncratic tail risk but cannot Gaussianize returns when the common factor is non-Gaussian. Third, we derive a joint Berry-Esseen bound showing Kolmogorov distance to Gaussian is O(T-1/2 + n-1/2), with explicit decomposition into time and cross-sectional error terms. We prove that for standardized time aggregation the Gaussian is the unique non-degenerate fixed point within the finite-variance class; for standardized asset aggregation the idiosyncratic component Gaussianizes while systematic factor laws are preserved fixed points at fixed horizon. The two aggregation paths do not commute at finite (T, n): diversify-thenhold yields different intermediate distributions than hold-then-diversify, with consequences for finite-sample risk assessment. The theory extends to long-memory volatility: when autocovariance decays as C V (h) ∼ h-α with α ∈ (0, 1), kurtosis decays as T-α rather than T-1 , implying slower convergencerelevant for rough volatility models. We connect results to Fokker-Planck dynamics, showing the spectral gap κ controls mixing while mean-reversion breaks scale invariance. For practitioners, we derive Cornish-Fisher VaR corrections from residual kurtosis. All rates are validated via Monte Carlo across CIR, log-OU, and multi-scale OU specifications.

title: Managing the World's Oil: Energy Dominance, Conditional Sovereignty, and the Reconfiguration of Global Power
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Managing the World's Oil: Energy Dominance, Conditional Sovereignty, and the Reconfiguration of Global Power
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the possibility that recent United States actions toward energy-rich, sanctioned states—most notably Venezuela and Iran—reflect an emerging approach to global energy governance centered on management, supervision, and conditional access rather than traditional regime change or territorial control. Situating these actions within a broader framework of “energy dominance,” the analysis explores whether control over oil revenue flows, maritime access, and financial settlement mechanisms is increasingly functioning as a primary instrument of geopolitical power.

Rather than treating Venezuela and Iran as isolated cases, the paper advances the interpretive claim that Venezuela may serve as a precedent through which externally supervised oil revenue management is normalized under the language of stabilization, accountability, and human rights enforcement. Within this framework, escalating pressure on Iran can be read as a potential extension of the same logic, in which fiscal sovereignty becomes contingent upon compliance with U.S.-led energy governance structures.

The paper further situates these dynamics within the context of intensifying strategic competition with China and Russia, arguing that oil operates not merely as a commodity but as infrastructural power underpinning currency stability, sanctions efficacy, and alliance formation. Particular attention is given to maritime enforcement, sanctions circumvention networks, and the increasing personalization of accountability directed at political leadership.

While acknowledging significant evidentiary limitations and refraining from claims of definitive intent or outcome, the analysis considers the structural incentives created by such an approach, including the delegation of management and enforcement functions to select U.S.-based entities and the temporal asymmetry through which the full implications of these arrangements may only become visible after political and legal constraints have lapsed.

By framing these developments as interpretive considerations rather than established facts, the paper seeks to illuminate a possible reconfiguration of global power in which energy management, rather than territorial control, becomes a central axis of geopolitical influence.

title: The Neo-Brandeisian Paradox: How Structural Antitrust Invites the Capture It Claims to Prevent

detail.title: The Neo-Brandeisian Paradox: How Structural Antitrust Invites the Capture It Claims to Prevent
detail.abstract:
Progressive antitrust reformers face a paradox: the structural remedies they propose would systematically invite the regulatory capture they claim to prevent. The Neo-Brandeisian movement—advocating bright-line market share presumptions, categorical prohibitions on vertical integration, and enforcement objectives beyond consumer welfare—seeks to constrain corporate power by expanding agency discretion. Public choice theory predicts this strategy will backfire.

This Article advances three novel contributions to the antitrust literature. First, it extends Judge Frank Easterbrook's error-cost framework to administrative agencies, identifying a tri-directional error problem unique to regulators: beyond false positives and false negatives, agencies face systematic policy oscillation as enforcement philosophies reverse with each administration—a cost Article III courts largely avoid. Second, it identifies a two-stage capture mechanism whereby structural expansion at the legislative stage invites procedural extraction at implementation, a pattern exemplified by the Magnuson-Moss Act. Third, it introduces the concept of "relationship capital"—bilateral interests between regulators and regulated firms that create durable resistance to institutional reform.

The evidence converges from multiple directions: historical analysis of 1950s–1970s structural enforcement, theoretical predictions from Stigler-Peltzman capture models, and contemporary documentation of antitrust threats deployed as content-moderation leverage in Murthy v. Missouri and related proceedings. Consumer welfare's evidentiary requirements, judicial enforceability, and single-metric constraint make it systematically more capture-resistant than structural alternatives.

The irony is stark: because concentrated interests organize more effectively than diffuse consumers, Neo-Brandeisian structural rules would likely entrench the very corporate dominance they oppose.

detail.abstract:
Poster for 'Bridging the Gap: Gender Pay, Financial Security and Literacy in India' presented in PAN India World Management Conference, IIM Ranchi (2025)

Abstract: India’s goal for Viksit Bharat @2047 focuses on financial inclusion as a means to foster economic and social advancement. A primary emphasis is enhancing financial literacy, particularly for women, to address persistent gender inequalities. Despite improvements in job participation and education levels, women in India continually earn lower wages than men in various sectors. This gender pay gap undermines women’s financial stability, limiting their ability to save, invest, and plan for retirement. Men in India generally face fewer barriers than women in wealth accumulation, investment, and financial security, largely due to higher earnings and better access to financial resources (PLFS, 2023). As according to National Sample Survey (NSS, 2021), only 23% of rural Indian women have a bank account, compared to 43% of men, highlighting disparities in financial access. Cultural standards, job segregation, and inadequate financial education exacerbate these disparities. This paper explores the impact of the pay gap on women’s financial security and views financial literacy as a key solution. Using 500 individuals, the study employs a (Difference-in-Differences) DiD approach which estimates the average effect of a financial literacy program on savings and financial security. Additionally, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) evaluates the lasting effects of salary disparities on economic well-being. It aims to provide policy suggestions to reduce wage disparity and enhance financial inclusion.

title: Governance & Guardrails: Artificial Intelligence and Low-Wage Workers
affiliations: UC Law, San Francisco

detail.title: Governance & Guardrails: Artificial Intelligence and Low-Wage Workers
detail.abstract: This Article examines an important, but undertheorized phenomenon at the intersection of technology and work: the rapidly increasing presence of artificial intelligence systems into low wage workplaces—and decidedly into the lives of low-wage workers themselves—and the resulting broader implications on work law and democracy. For decades, technology has enabled employers to increasingly exert control over workers; but for all their promise, emerging technologies like artificial intelligence also extend a new and potentially harmful level of concern for low-wage workers in particular.1From algorithmic software that unilaterally determines workers’ schedules “on demand” and without notice; to constant and often surreptitious surveillance and monitoring of workers’ every move; to the quiet, often invisible collection of workers’ data, AI-powered workplace technologies have, in their quest to maximize productivity, in the process minimized workers’ rights. Absent guardrails to govern their use, these technologies purport to optimize labor while in fact harming low-wage workers and eroding the institution of work. For the few unionized low-wage workers that enjoy collectively bargained contract provisions, those that expressly address technology in the workplace are beneficial (and instructive). But for the vast majority—the tens of millions of low-wage workers who are not unionized—few legal or regulatory vehicles exist that offer them a voice into, or protection against, how such technologies affect their working conditions or their lives. Where formal labor representation has proved elusive to ninety-four percent of low- wage workers in the private sector,2alternate structural formations have emerged that provide low-wage workers with some semblance of collective voice in the workplace: worker centers, community coalitions, and labor- community partnerships. Together these enable a “co-enforcement” model— a formal partnership between government and workers which can help solve for this challenge,3and aid in the nascent but growing movement to establish meaningful workplace technology rights.4 This Article 1) directly confronts how this new technological paradigm affects the nearly 26 million low-wage workers5whose working conditions, livelihoods, and lives are most vulnerable; and 2) enumerates a framework for meaningful governance and guardrails to mitigate harms to low-wage workers caused by employers’ use of these technologies.

title: Value vs. Growth: What Drives the Value Premium?
affiliations: University of Idaho,  and Washington State University

detail.title: Value vs. Growth: What Drives the Value Premium?
detail.abstract: Each year, a significant number of stocks transition from non-value stocks to value stocks and likewise from non-growth stocks to growth stocks. As a result, about half of value stocks and half of growth stocks are new. We find that the value premium based on new value and growth stocks is statistically higher than that based on old value and growth stocks, mostly driven by the underperformance of new growth stocks. In addition, we find that the large value premium for new value and growth stocks is more pronounced during contraction, Fed monetary tightening cycle, subperiods with high long-term yields, and high economic uncertainty. Moreover, we show that the large value premium for new value and growth stocks is mainly the across-industry effect. Finally, international evidence further confirms the findings.

title: Common Analysts as Facilitators and Screeners in M&A Deals
affiliations: Georgia State University and Peking University HSBC Business School

detail.title: Common Analysts as Facilitators and Screeners in M&A Deals
detail.abstract: We examine the role of common analysts-analysts who cover both the acquirer and the targetin mergers and acquisitions. We find that analysts shared by firm pairs increase deal announcement likelihoods between them, particularly when uncertainty about stand-alone valuations and the potential for synergies is high. Deals involving them are more likely to be stock-financed and less likely to include target termination agreements. Furthermore, deal completion is less likely, suggesting that they do more than merely facilitate transactions. Post-announcement acquirer recommendation changes by them have a stronger effect on completion outcomes than those by acquirer stand-alone analysts. They are associated with more competitive bidding and higher deal failure rates driven by pricing disputes or adverse acquirer valuation effects. Conditional on deal completion, they are linked to higher combined and acquirer announcement-period returns and lower target returns. Overall, common analysts serve dual roles as both deal facilitators and screeners.

title: Why Successful Large Organisations Behave Strangely: How Large Organisations Stay Aligned Under Pressure
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Why Successful Large Organisations Behave Strangely: How Large Organisations Stay Aligned Under Pressure
detail.abstract:
Some large organisations remain aligned to their intent despite sustained pressure from scale, complexity, and uncertainty. In doing so, they often behave in ways that appear inefficient, irrational, or strategically questionable when judged against standard management logic. They refuse profitable opportunities, impose hard constraints, absorb costs competitors externalise, or deliberately limit optionality. Such behaviours are commonly described as unusual, risky, or counterintuitive.

This paper examines that pattern. It asks: how do some large organisations remain aligned to their intent under pressure, and why does that alignment often look strange?

Drawing on case studies across retail, manufacturing, and deep technology—including Costco, Woolworths, Toyota, BYD, ASML, and TSMC—the paper uses Attention Over the Loop (ATOL) as a diagnostic grammar for interpreting organisational behaviour. Rather than explaining outcomes or prescribing practices, ATOL renders behaviour intelligible by showing how organisations arrange the structural conditions required for learning under ontological difficulty.

Through this lens, behaviours that initially appear inefficient or risky become legible as deliberate choices about where to locate pain, authority, responsibility, freedom, and attention. The organisations examined repeatedly choose internal discomfort over external relief, learning inefficiency over short-term gain, and constraint over flexibility in order to remain anchored to reality and intent. Alignment under pressure is shown not to be a function of culture or optimisation, but the visible cost of maintaining learning structures where they would otherwise fragment by default.

title: YYA Glossary | Paradigm
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: YYA Glossary | Paradigm
detail.abstract: Paradigm, as used by Yuen Yuen Ang, is a system of thought grounded in core assumptions about the nature of societies that determines what questions are asked and what concepts, theories, and methods are created and used. In contrast to a theory (an answer to a particular question), a paradigm is a way of seeing and studying the social world—akin to an operating system, in which core assumptions function as the source code. A paradigm should not be conflated with a framework, which refers to a organizational checklist that does not redefine underlying assumptions. Ang’s AIM Political Economy is a paradigm, not a framework.

title: Imploring Urgent Legislative Reinstatement of ‘Tax Residency Certificate’: Reflections on Supreme Court of India’s Decision in Tiger Global
affiliations: Supreme Court of India

detail.title: Imploring Urgent Legislative Reinstatement of ‘Tax Residency Certificate’: Reflections on Supreme Court of India’s Decision in Tiger Global
detail.abstract:
In its recent decision in Tiger Global case, the Supreme Court of India has declared that Tax Residency Certificates (TRCs) issued by foreign Competent Authority is not sufficient to conclude upon residential status of a person claiming benefit of bilateral tax treaty with India. This marks reversal of long settled legal position.

This paper argues that the legal position flowing from this declaration needs to be revisited and greater legitimacy needs to be conferred upon TRCs issued by foreign competent authorities. The paper spells out the consequences of the determination that TRC is not conclusive proof of residence of the taxpayer and suggests recalibration by reinstituting the status of TRCs albeit under a joint-investigation mechanism manned by competent authorities of both countries.

title: Nested Search
affiliations: Northwestern University

detail.title: Nested Search
detail.abstract: I introduce and study a nested search problem modeled as a tree structure that generalizes Weitzman (1979) in two ways: (1) search progresses incrementally, reflecting real-life scenarios where agents gradually acquire information about the prizes; and (2) the realization of prizes can be correlated, capturing similarities among them. I derive the optimal policy, which takes the form of an index solution. I apply this result to study monopolistic competition in a market with two stages of product inspection. My application illustrates that regulations on drip pricing lower equilibrium price and raise consumer surplus.
