detail.abstract: Chinese biotech companies are licensing billions in drug patents to Western pharmaceutical giants. This seismic shift reveals both the maturation of China's innovation ecosystem and the precarious economics forcing many promising startups to sell their crown jewels. In May 2025, something remarkable happened in the pharmaceutical world. Pfizer agreed to pay $1.25 billion upfront, with potential milestone payments reaching $6 billion, for a single experimental cancer drug from 3SBio, a company based in Shenyang, China. Two months later, GlaxoSmithKline struck an even larger deal: up to $12 billion to license a dozen innovative medicines from Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals. These weren't isolated transactions. They were the leading edge of a pharmaceutical revolution that is fundamentally reshaping how the world's medicines are discovered and developed.

title: Spin City: Local Externalities of Wind Turbines
affiliations: , Friedrich-Alexander-University Erlangen-Nürnberg and University of Cologne

detail.title: Spin City: Local Externalities of Wind Turbines
detail.abstract: Wind turbines offer significant environmental benefits but also create negative local externalities, such as noise and visual pollution, which can lead to local tensions and community resistance against the energy transition. This paper examines negative and positive externalities associated with wind turbine siting in Germany. Utilizing an instrumental variables approach, we find that wind turbine siting decreases house purchase prices by 1.9% in affected municipalities, with this adverse effect being most pronounced for the first turbines installed. Additionally, the siting of wind turbines reduces local tourism, apartment rents, and leads to fewer building permits being issued for apartments and houses, exacerbating existing housing shortages. On the positive side, each installed wind turbine increases a municipality's local tax capacity by 1.8\% through higher commercial tax revenues. Our findings suggest that the negative externalities can be mitigated by investing the increased tax revenue into local amenities and public services, thereby compensating for the adverse effects of wind turbines.

title: Entry Threat and Supra-competitive Pricing in Homogeneous-Goods Markets
affiliations: Wenlan School of Business, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law and Wenlan School of Business, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law

detail.title: Entry Threat and Supra-competitive Pricing in Homogeneous-Goods Markets
detail.abstract: We study a homogeneous-goods market with two identical incumbent suppliers, a potential entrant, and multiple downstream retailers. A market price is supra-competitive if it exceeds the incumbents' competitive equilibrium price in the absence of entry. We show that supra-competitive market prices arise only in exclusionary equilibria: the incumbents raise prices to generate profits required to finance transfers that induce retailers not to accommodate entry. Exclusion can occur even when the entrant is highly efficient or transfers are small. These qualitative results extend to an asymmetric-information setting in which the entrant's unit cost is privately known.

title: Though You Are Insignificant in Your Own Eyes: The Rise and Fall of Western Civilization's Foundational Government
affiliations: Economic Roundtable

detail.title: Though You Are Insignificant in Your Own Eyes: The Rise and Fall of Western Civilization's Foundational Government
detail.abstract: The biblical account of King Saul and Israel's transition from a loose tribal confederation to a centralized state is a foundational text for Western political and religious thought, influencing ideas about leadership, law, and governance. Saul reveled in public praise. He sought to enhance his own reputation rather than fulfill the deeper responsibilities of kingship. His failed journey shows that the arc of grandiosity bends toward hubris. The malevolent giant Goliath embodied the chaos monster within Saul, rendering him incapable of fighting on behalf of the forces of order. He sought control, yet under his control the world became a more dangerous place, and the more he controlled it the more terrifying it became for him. He was unable to contain the tensions of conflict, sacrifice, loss, and remorse that were interwoven with the power of his position. Societies governed by narcissists, including the United States, risk the normalization of unethical behavior. They decay from within as trust, collaboration, and integrity are replaced by paranoia, fear, and a cult of personality. The story is a reflective mirror for governments struggling with legitimacy and morality. It shows the need for integrity, self-understanding, trust, adaptability, empathy, accountability, and transparency.

title: The Incompatibility of the Condorcet Winner and Loser Criteria With Positive or Negative Involvement and Resolvability

detail.title: The Incompatibility of the Condorcet Winner and Loser Criteria With Positive or Negative Involvement and Resolvability
detail.abstract: We prove that there is no preferential voting method satisfying the Condorcet winner and loser criteria, positive involvement (if a candidate x wins in an initial preference profile, then adding a voter who ranks x uniquely first cannot cause x to lose), and n-voter resolvability (if x initially ties for winning, then x can be made the unique winner by adding some set of up to n voters). This impossibility theorem holds for any positive integer n. In addition, positive involvement can be replaced by negative involvement (if a candidate x loses in an initial preference profile, then adding a voter who ranks x uniquely last cannot cause x to win). In a previous note, we proved an analogous result assuming an additional axiom of ordinal margin invariance, which we now show is unnecessary for an impossibility theorem, at least if the desired voting method is defined for five-candidate elections.

title: Empowering Pakistan's Cities: Completing the 18th Amendment's Bottom-Up Promise in 2026

detail.title: Empowering Pakistan's Cities: Completing the 18th Amendment's Bottom-Up Promise in 2026
detail.abstract: Pakistan's cities generate 55% GDP but face acute governance deficits exposed by COVID-19. The 18th Amendment (2010) devolved powers to provinces yet stalled at Provincial Finance Commissions, leaving cities like Lahore and Karachi under-resourced amid 38% urbanization. FAFEN's 2025 constitutional reforms and 2026's "year of reforms" under PM Shehbaz Sharif offer political momentum to complete this devolution. Key recommendations: Activate PFCs with Medium-Term Budgetary Frameworks; strengthen municipal data aligned with SDGs; reverse civil service posting patterns to retain talent locally. COVID proved local governance capacity matters; 2026 provides the window. Without immediate city empowerment, future pandemics, climate shocks, and security threats will overwhelm fragile urban institutions, threatening national stability.

title: Facilitating the Future of Computing Education: The Role of the 2026-2030 NSF Strategic Plan toward Equipping Educators and Students for the Post-AI World
affiliations: University of Illinois Chicago, University of Illinois System and University of Illinois System

detail.title: Facilitating the Future of Computing Education: The Role of the 2026-2030 NSF Strategic Plan toward Equipping Educators and Students for the Post-AI World
detail.abstract: High-quality STEM education and competencies in computing fundamentals are foundational for enabling a pipeline of skilled graduates for the computing-centric jobs that will define the future American economy. Also required is the continual development of educators to meet future STEM needs through regular professional development. Our collective work as researchers, technology developers, and computing educators focuses on developing educational technologies for STEM education and equipping educators with computing and AI skills. There is a strong need for rapidly developed, but robust evidence on the use of AI-and computingbased approaches to support students across all disciplines in the development of core technology skills that will be necessary to succeed in today's AI-ubiquitous world. We applaud the dedication to STEM education in the draft 2026-2030 NSF Strategic Plan, as without a strong presence of STEM education from PreK to college and beyond, America will struggle with keeping up with workforce demands in science and technology industries. Furthermore, STEM education benefits all students, regardless of chosen career, as it instills powerful thinking, reasoning, and analysis skills that are valuable in working in high-paying jobs as well as navigating everyday life. We, as individual researchers and educators in computing and AI, submit the following comments in response to the request for feedback on the 2026-2030 NSF Strategic Plan, based on feedback areas sought by NSF.

title: Impact of An Infrastructure Failure on Cognitive Performance

detail.title: Impact of An Infrastructure Failure on Cognitive Performance
detail.abstract: Natural and human-made disasters can have far-reaching impacts on health and human capital for affected individuals. The 2007 collapse of the I-35W Mississippi River Bridge in Minneapolis, Minnesota, led to a substantial disruption of the learning environment for students in affected communities. The collapse resulted in numerous fatalities and injuries; notably, a school bus carrying 63 students was on the bridge during the collapse, and traffic patterns were disrupted for a year. Using a two-way fixed effects and synthetic difference-indifferences approach, I find that the bridge collapse leads to lower standardized test scores for affected schools relative to similar unaffected schools. Furthermore, I provide evidence that improvements in air quality due to reduced traffic do not outweigh the trauma-induced psychological stress impacts of the disaster.

title: Digital Financial Colonialism?
affiliations: University of Johanneburg

detail.title: Digital Financial Colonialism?
detail.abstract: Digital finance is widely promoted as a pathway to financial inclusion, economic empowerment, and development across the Global South. This paper challenges such narratives by arguing that fintech-led inclusion has generated a new form of structural dependency best described as Digital Financial Colonialism. Drawing on theories of data colonialism, surveillance capitalism, and critical political economy, the paper conceptualises how externally owned digital financial infrastructures enable data extraction, algorithmic governance, and the erosion of economic and data sovereignty. It develops a conceptual framework identifying three core mechanisms: data extraction and external value capture, algorithmic governance of credit and risk, and structural dependency arising from platform dominance. The analysis demonstrates that inclusion focused primarily on access, without ownership, data rights, and regulatory capacity, risks reproducing extractive relationships in digital form. The paper concludes that digital financial inclusion, if poorly governed, may deepen inequality and constrain policy autonomy, and calls for development strategies that prioritise data sovereignty, algorithmic accountability, and domestic institutional capacity.

title: Hide Your Strength, Bide Your Time? China's International Monetary Strategy at the Crossroads
affiliations: New York University Shanghai and Global Climate Forum

detail.title: Hide Your Strength, Bide Your Time? China's International Monetary Strategy at the Crossroads

publicationDetails.detailsText: OBFA-TRANSFORM Working Paper N0. 14-EN, February 2026

detail.abstract: The weaponization of dollar-based financial infrastructure following Russia's invasion of Ukraine has made China's hedging strategy against dollar dependence more visible to outside observers. However, the architecture of that strategy was put in place years earlier. This article argues that China's international monetary strategy underwent a decisive pivot between 2014 and 2016-triggered by the capital flight episode that demonstrated the dangers of rapid financial opening, not by post-2022 sanctions risks. Drawing on the Global Credit View (GCV), which analyses gross balance sheet positions rather than net flows, we trace the development of China's international monetary strategy since the beginning of the Reform and Opening Up period in 1978, illustrating how China abandoned its capital account liberalization agenda following the 2015 exchange rate reform, replaced passive reserve accumulation with active diversification through policy banks and sovereign funds, and constructed alternative settlement infrastructure (CIPS, offshore RMB centres, swap line networks). By analysing China's flow-of-funds data, we show that reserve assets now constitute approximately 43% of China's total external portfolio, with the remainder held through diversified state vehicles largely invisible in conventional analyses. Current efforts to promote RMB internationalization-including the digital yuan and mBridge-represent continuations and accelerants of this earlier shift, not merely responses to recent geopolitical tensions. We characterize this strategy as "defensive internationalization": expanding RMB usage through offshore nodes while maintaining capital controls onshore. This may provide China with monetary sovereignty to pursue its economic rise without full exposure to dollar-system vulnerabilities, though it is unlikely to displace the hegemony of the U.S. dollar in international trade and finance.

title: Thirst for Talent: Competition in the Hiring of High-skilled Workers
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management, Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management, Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management

detail.title: Thirst for Talent: Competition in the Hiring of High-skilled Workers
detail.abstract: We examine how Chinese firms compete for high-skilled talent using novel text-based product market competitor networks and job posting data. We document strong strategic complementarity: a one unit increase in rivals' high-skilled postings raises a firm's own postings by 0.6. This competition is product-market driven, national in scope, and absent for low-skilled workers. A theoretical model shows complementarity arises when the fear of falling behind outweighs the gain from leading. Our results indicate that talent competition amplifies labor demand and is a central channel for product-market rivalry.

detail.abstract: The paper discusses the future of plant-based nutrition in sports and its potential to replace traditional whey-based protein supplementation. The main focus is on how plant-based diets affect athletic performance, recovery, and sustainability. This is an important topic because now a days athletes are seeking an healthy, ethical, and environmentally friendly nutrition option that will support their peak performance. The survey was conducted among more than 100 athletes, gym-goers, trainers, and shopkeepers, based on research taken from academic studies and real-life examples such as Virat Kohli and Serena Williams, stated that though whey protein remains on top due to its taste and assured results, but the interest in plant-based proteins is slowly rising. However, taste, cost, and lack of awareness are significant barriers to wider diffusion. The study identified that, with innovation, education, and improvement in quality, plant-based proteins can emerge as a strong and sustainable alternative, contributing toward the health of the athletes and the future of the planet.

detail.abstract: Social media has become an important marketing tool for startups in today's digital age. Startups often have limited financial and human resources, so they depend on social media platforms to reach customers and promote their products and services. This research paper studies the role of social media in startup customer acquisition. The study is based on primary data collected from 100 respondents through a structured questionnaire. The research examines how social media platforms help startups in creating brand awareness, engaging with customers, building trust, and influencing purchase decisions. The findings show that social media platforms such as Instagram and Facebook are most effective in attracting customers due to their wide reach and interactive features. The study also identifies several challenges faced by startups, including content creation, limited manpower, and difficulty in measuring return on investment. Despite these challenges, the research concludes that social media is a cost-effective and powerful tool for customer acquisition. With proper planning and regular engagement, startups can successfully use social media to grow their business.

title: Beyond the Rational Agent: A Behavioral Critique of Economic Modeling
affiliations: and International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM)

detail.title: Beyond the Rational Agent: A Behavioral Critique of Economic Modeling
detail.abstract: Standard neoclassical economic models rely heavily on the assumption of Homo Economicus-a rational, utility-maximizing agent operating within efficient markets. This paper challenges the universal applicability of such models, particularly within the context of volatile and transitional economies. By integrating principles from behavioral economics with empirical observations from Damascus, Syria, and Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, this study isolates specific cognitive biases that drive market deviations. The analysis contrasts the "Scarcity Heuristic" observed in hyper-inflationary environments-where panic buying acts as a rational hedge-against the "Veblen Effect" in high-growth emerging markets, where social signaling inverts standard demand curves. The findings suggest that "irrational" behaviors are often adaptive survival mechanisms, indicating that monetary policy in developing nations must account for psychological variables such as loss aversion and status-seeking to be effective.

title: Global Value Chains and Informality
affiliations: University of Warwick - Warwick Manufacturing Group, International Labour Organization (ILO), Aarhus University - Department of Economics and Business Economics and International Labour Organization (ILO)

detail.title: Global Value Chains and Informality
detail.abstract: Taking advantage of a novel sample of 34 industries covering almost the entire economies of 76 developed and less developed countries in 1995-2019, we identify how participation in Global Value Chains (GVCs) through linkages with suppliers (i.e., backward) and buyers (i.e., forward) and their interplays with development, institutions, skill endowments, and innovation capabilities relate to the shares of self-employment, informal work, and informal-sector (i.e., informal and household) work. Results likely point to complementarities among the generation of domestic value added that is supplied through GVCs, institutional quality, skills, experience and expertise, innovation, utilisation of advanced technologies, and formal employment. While they also likely point to complementarities among the sourcing and incorporation of foreign value added in industries' exports through GVCs, institutional quality, generic skills, exported product quality, and formal employment, complementarities among this activity, innovation, managerial and professional skills, experience and expertise, and formal employment are non-existent.

title: Flexibility or Structure? A Comparison of Customer Service User Experiences with LLM-Based and Intent-Based Conversational AI
affiliations: SINTEF Digital, Telenor, SINTEF Digital, SINTEF Digital, Independent, boost.ai and SINTEF Digital

detail.title: Flexibility or Structure? A Comparison of Customer Service User Experiences with LLM-Based and Intent-Based Conversational AI
detail.abstract: Conversational AI is increasingly used in customer service and related domains, yet design approaches differ substantially. Intent-based conversational AI often relies on scripted pathways and structured options, offering clarity and predictability, while systems based on large language models (LLM) generate free-text responses that allow greater flexibility and human-likeness. While these approaches may have their individual strengths and weaknesses, there is a lack of studies comparing user experiences in the customer service context. This paper presents two studies comparing user experiences with these approaches in the telecom domain. In Study 1 (N = 226), participants interacted with either an LLM-or an intent-based conversational AI and evaluated their experiences. In Study 2 (N = 172), participants used both systems and indicated their preference. Quantitative results from Study 1 showed no significant differences between the two systems. Qualitative analyses revealed complementary strengths: the LLM-based system was valued for flexibility, detailed explanations, and tone, while the intent-based system was appreciated for structure, ease of navigation, and concise information. In Study 2, user preferences were nearly evenly split between the two systems (55% vs. 45%) and impacted by task type and interaction order, underscoring the situational character of system fit. Taken together, the findings suggest that user satisfaction may not depend on the absolute superiority of one approach but on alignment between system characteristics and situational needs. We discuss implications for conversational AI design, emphasizing hybrid approaches that combine LLM adaptability with intent-based structure.

title: Co-Branded Credit Cards as a Credit Gateway: Retail Demand Effects of First-Time Credit Access
affiliations: University of Notre Dame - Mendoza College of Business, Rice University - Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business and Northwestern University - Department of Marketing

detail.title: Co-Branded Credit Cards as a Credit Gateway: Retail Demand Effects of First-Time Credit Access
detail.abstract: Co-branded credit cards are widely used by retailers to strengthen customer relationships and increase demand. We study the retailer-demand effects of first-time credit access in Peru by leveraging a temporary underwriting pilot that extended credit to applicants with no or limited formal credit history. Linking credit decisions to item-level transactions at a large multi-banner retailer, we find that card approval nearly doubles monthly spending at the partner retailer. A decomposition of the spending response shows that this lift is driven primarily by increased shopping frequency (64%), with smaller contributions from basket size (27%) and the average price paid per item (9%). Credit access induces purchases in new product categories, whereas retailer-controlled, cardholder-exclusive promotions account for a sizable share of the aggregate lift by deepening spending within existing categories. Consumers with prior credit access exhibit qualitatively similar but substantially smaller responses. Together, these findings show that a retailer that expands access to formal credit may capture a significant and persistent share of ongoing demand through increased store traffic.

title: Malignant Whispers: Turmoil in a Public Organization
affiliations: Economic Roundtable

detail.title: Malignant Whispers: Turmoil in a Public Organization
detail.abstract: Public organizations have complex and sometimes contradictory mandates. Political change, especially large swings, can churn these mandates, making them less consistent and coherent. The personal values of employees may already diverge from official directives. Large, abrupt, multi-pronged policy swings can expand the gulf between personal values and organizational mandates from manageable tension to unmanageable bedlam. This article examines how the dynamics of collective dysfunction in institutions parallel the disorganization of thought, feeling, and meaning observed in schizophrenia. It explores fragmentation, delusional control, moral inversion, and the loss of historicity as structural processes that mirror the pathology of schizophrenia. The dynamics of collective dysfunction in a beleaguered public agency are mapped by documenting internal disorder, confusion of purpose, and interpersonal failures. Participantobservation is augmented by textual and symbolic interpretation to uncover patterns of denial, projection, and fragmentation that rendered the organization incapable of coherent functioning. These patterns are shown to resemble the symptoms of schizophrenia-specifically, disorganization of thought, ambivalence, emotional disengagement, and loss of historic continuity. The failure of bureaucracies to think coherently, communicate authentically, or sustain purpose reflects at a social level the same breakdown of integration that characterizes schizophrenia. Schizophrenia is a metaphor for loss of relatedness and meaning that can inform efforts to repair dysfunctional organizations.

title: Defining Socially Assistive Robots for the Law: Preliminary Results of a Systematic Review
affiliations: Universiteit Leiden, eLaw, Leiden University and Leiden University - Center for Law and Digital Technologies

detail.title: Defining Socially Assistive Robots for the Law: Preliminary Results of a Systematic Review

publicationDetails.detailsText: In: Palinko, O., et al. (eds.) Social Robotics: 16th International Conference, ICSR + AI 2024, Odense, Denmark, October 23–26, 2024 Lecture Notes in Computer Science nr. 15563, Springer, p. 268-278.

detail.abstract: Over the past two decades, socially assistive (SARs) or interactive (SIRs) robots have been developed rapidly due to their beneficial uses in elderly care, rehabilitation, and education. Given their multiple embodiments and contexts of use, however, defining what these robots are remains a difficult task, which further challenges understanding which legal safeguards developers need to follow to ensure a safe human-robot interaction (HRI). Establishing legislation that adequately frames the issues is complex if these concepts remain confusing. Despite pioneer efforts to characterize what these robots are in international standards and the literature, there is currently no consensus on which legal category they are, and, therefore, related problems are covered unevenly in different pieces of legislation. Following a systematic review, we analyzed 1,359 wo rks (out of 3,446) to clarify definitions, categories, and functionalities of SARs and SIRs to establish a baseline for understanding and regulating these robots. The first results show that the ISO 13482:2014 definition of Mobile Service Robots (MSRs), the formal name for SARs, is incompatible with the current literature. Moreover, more consensus on what qualifies as assistive or interactive under this technology is needed to determine the regulation and safeguards to mitigate the issues these robots entail for users Keywords: socially assistive robots • socially interactive robots • social robots • la w • personal care • systematic review

title: Implementation of Automated Intelligent Note Routing at a Cancer Center: A Socio-technical Change Perspective
affiliations: Florida International University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Florida International University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Florida International University (FIU)

detail.title: Implementation of Automated Intelligent Note Routing at a Cancer Center: A Socio-technical Change Perspective
detail.abstract: ObjectiveTo analyze the implementation process of the Automated Intelligent Note Routing (AINR) system at a cancer center and its operational impact from a sociotechnical change management perspective.MethodsThis longitudinal, mixed-methods study describes the implementation of AINR within a cancer center. Data collected during pre-, mid-, and post-implementation phases spanned 3.5 years. Qualitative data included stakeholder interviews, workflow observations, and project documentation. Quantitative data included system audit logs, transmission reports, and operational metrics on efficiency, accuracy, timeliness, and labor utilization. Analyses focused on changes across technical, workflow, data, and organizational dimensions.ResultsAINR replaced manual fax-based note routing with automated detection and rule-based delivery of signed clinical notes. Average note processing time dropped from 10–15 minutes to seconds per note, a reduction of over 95%. Monthly staff hours spent on note routing decreased by 90%, enabling redeployment to higher-value tasks. Misrouted notes fell from around 10% to 1%. Conservative labor cost estimates indicated savings exceeding $169,000 over the first 14 months. Persistent failures were primarily attributable to organizational issues, such as missing providers and provider opt-outs, rather than to technical constraints.ConclusionWhile automation provided significant efficiency and accuracy, successful implementation relied on redesigning workflows, clarifying roles, establishing data governance, and maintaining ongoing change management. A sociotechnical approach showed organizational alignment, not just technology, was key to lasting improvement. AINR demonstrates that enhancing clinical documentation exchange in complex healthcare environments requires combining technical automation with intentional organizational strategies to achieve scalable and sustainable results.

title: Emotional Dynamics: The Nonlinear Impact of Sentiment Volatility on Review Helpfulness
affiliations: , The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen - School of Management and Economics, The University of Texas at Austin and Zhejiang University - School of Management

detail.title: Emotional Dynamics: The Nonlinear Impact of Sentiment Volatility on Review Helpfulness
detail.abstract: Affective cues embedded in online reviews play a pivotal role in shaping perceptions of review helpfulness. While prior research has primarily examined static affective characteristics (e.g., valence and arousal, discrete emotions, presence of mixed emotions), they have overlooked the fact that emotional expressions often fluctuate throughout the textual flow. Addressing this gap, this research introduces sentiment volatility as a novel dynamic cue for understanding mixedemotion reviews. Drawing on emotions as social information (EASI) theory, we theorize that sentiment volatility influences perceived review helpfulness through both affective and inferential processes. We employ a multimethod approach involving (1) an analysis of a realworld dataset, (2) a functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) experiment, and (3) an online experiment. Across these studies, we consistently find an inverted U-shaped relationship between 2 sentiment volatility and perceived review helpfulness. This relationship is jointly driven by emotional contagion (reflecting affective engagement) and perceived reviewer rationality (reflecting inferential reasoning). Moreover, emotional susceptibility (ES) moderates both mediating pathways, such that the effects of sentiment volatility are amplified among individuals with higher ES. Our findings advance existing literature by extending both research streams on affective characteristics and mixed-emotion review from static to dynamic perspectives and provide practical implications for platforms and merchants.

title: Still Packing a Punch
affiliations: , International Monetary Fund, International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund

detail.title: Still Packing a Punch

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper assesses the transmission of monetary policy using a new state-of-the-art intra-day dataset of monetary policy shocks for 16 advanced economies and emerging markets, the most comprehensive cross-country coverage to date. Using 30-minute windows around policy announcements, we construct target and path factor shocks for a broad sample of countries and assess their transmission to  government bond yields, stock prices, and exchange rates. High-frequency identification improves the significance of estimated responses relative to lower-frequency intraday or daily data. Both target and path surprises generate large and consistent effects across asset classes. We find limited evidence of central bank information effects, confirming the validity of high-frequency methods. Post-COVID-19, transmission to yields and equity prices remains stable, but exchange rate responses weaken—likely due to synchronized monetary tightening across countries. The findings underscore the value of high-frequency data for robust identification and cross-country analysis of monetary policy transmission.

title: Beyond Binary

detail.title: Beyond Binary

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the FinOpen index, a novel measure of capital flow management for 193 countries from 1996 to 2022. Using information from the IMF’s Annual Report on Exchange Arrangements and Exchange Restrictions (AREAER), the index is constructed by estimating the level of openness annually and updating it daily by incorporating changes in capital flow management measures (CFMs). Therefore, this index goes beyond the traditional indexes that rely on binary labels that only distinguish between full capital openness and any control. Within the range of [0, 1], the FinOpen index quantifies granular policy intensity and allows comparisons across countries (with higher values indicate greater capital openness). In addition, the dataset extends back to 1960 for 42 emerging and developing countries, and the methodology can be applied to construct long-term series for other countries.

title: Banking on Nonbanks
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and

detail.title: Banking on Nonbanks

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study how banking groups adjust corporate credit supply in response to tighter macroprudential policies. Using granular data on syndicated corporate loans, we show that banking groups reallocate lending from bank subsidiaries toward affiliated nonbank financial institutions (NBFIs) following regulatory tightening. Relative to bank subsidiaries within the same group, NBFI subsidiaries expand lending, and their credit supply also increases in absolute terms. We estimate that by ‘banking on’ their nonbanks, banking groups offset, on average, more than half of the contraction in bank lending induced by macroprudential tightening. Our findings highlight an important intra-group reallocation channel through which banking groups can partially offset regulatory constraints and result in greater bank–nonbank interconnectedness.

title: Understanding and Forecasting Inflation in Timor-Leste
affiliations: and International Monetary Fund

detail.title: Understanding and Forecasting Inflation in Timor-Leste

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of inflation in Timor-Leste—a post-conflict, low-income economy and small developing state that is fully dollarized. We find that Timorese inflation was high until about mid-2010 and was strongly influenced by swings in global food prices given its high share of food in the CPI basket and heavy reliance on food imports. But inflation has been relatively low and stable in the past decade relative to peers—a period that also broadly coincided with moderate global food prices. We develop an empirical model for Timorese inflation that distills the role of these underlying drivers, and which can be deployed for forecasting inflation.

title: Distributional Impacts of Inflation Accounting for Behavioral Effects and Real Assets
affiliations: , International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Distributional Impacts of Inflation Accounting for Behavioral Effects and Real Assets

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the redistributive effects of inflation across 18 European economies from 2021:Q3 to 2022:Q2, using unique micro-datasets for this country sample. We estimate inflation’s impact on household welfare through the consumption basket, income, and wealth channels. Our main contribution is incorporating real assets into the wealth channel and accounting for behavioral responses to inflation in both the income and wealth channels. These factors significantly alter inflation’s distributional effects compared to previous literature. The inflation shock is estimated to have caused an average welfare loss equivalent to 18.5 percent of annual household income across our sample, with households in the poorest income quintiles suffering the largest losses. Cross-country differences also widen when real assets are incorporated, with a few economies even showing welfare gains for some or all quintiles because house prices rose faster than inflation.

title: Model Risk Under CECL: A Consumer Finance Perspective
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia

detail.title: Model Risk Under CECL: A Consumer Finance Perspective

keywords: Allowance for Loan and Lease Losses

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Philadelphia Working Paper No. 26-9
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine the challenges of economic forecasting and model misspecification errors confronted by financial institutions implementing the novel current expected credit loss (CECL) allowance methodology and its impact on model risk and bias in CECL projections. We document the increased sensitivity to model and macroeconomic forecasting error of the CECL framework with respect to the incurred loss framework that it replaces. An empirical application illustrates how to leverage simple machine learning (ML) strategies and statistical principles in the design of a nimble and flexible CECL modeling framework. We show that, even in consumer loan portfolios with tens of millions of loans, like mortgage, auto, or credit card portfolios, one can develop, estimate, and deploy an array of models quickly and efficiently, and without a forecasting performance penalty. Drawing on more than 20 years of auto loans data and the experience from the Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic, we leverage basic econometric principles to identify strategies to deal with biased model projections in times of high economic uncertainty. We advocate for a focus on resiliency and adaptability of models and model infrastructures to novel shocks and uncertain economic conditions.
